## What this market taught me

**The company screen is doing exactly what the log says it does, and it is the binding filter — but
it is not the only one, and it was not the main one this time.** Of 28 rows, eight clear every
must-have. Seven of the twenty parked rows fail on **must-have 8** (no company identity anywhere),
but **nine fail on must-have 2** — mole checks, mole mapping, dermoscopy, thread and leg vein work,
sclerotherapy, minor surgery. That is the single biggest cause of rule-outs in this sweep, ahead of
the company screen, and it matches what the brief says about New Zealand small towns: an English
secondary town cannot support a pure injectables menu either, so the clinics bolt on vein and
lesion work. **Screen the menu first in the UK too; it is not just an antipodean pattern.**

**The 22 Oct correction holds, and can now be stated more strongly.** Every one of the eight
sendable rows published a readable address, and so did almost every clinic that failed on the menu.
The two qualifications are independent, and the sweep adds a second independence worth noting:
**tidiness of site does not predict legal form either.** The only clinic that printed both its
company name and number on its own page — Skin Aesthetics Clinic in Reading — has placeholder
"Learn more" links and no named owner, while Taunton Aesthetics, the most professionally built site
in the sweep with three priced membership programmes and a named nurse, turns out to have **no
company at all**.

**The one-call-per-town advanced search is still the right order, and it got cheaper to use once I
found its two failure modes.** Nineteen town calls answered must-have 8 and must-have 4 together for
whole markets, and **not one privacy policy was read all run**. But: (1) `companyNameIncludes`
matches **whole words, not substrings** — `aesthetic` returns only companies with "AESTHETIC" as a
standalone word and MISSES every "AESTHETICS" name. My first six town calls were nearly wasted
before I switched to `aesthetics`; **always use the plural**. (2) It **truncates at 20 results per
page** and big towns overflow — Bolton returned 77, Colchester 38, Northampton 29, Wigan 32 — so in
a large town the clinic you want can be paginated off page 1 and read as absent. Bodywise Skin
Clinic in Bolton was invisible that way and only surfaced on a targeted name search. **Treat a
no-match in a town that returned 20-of-N as unresolved, not as negative.**

**Targeted name searches are the better second call, and they are decisive in both directions.**
Seven of them resolved five clinics outright — Lincoln Aesthetic, Exthetics, Mid Yorkshire Skin
Clinic and Bodywise Skin Clinic each turned out to have **its registered office at the clinic's own
published address**, which is the strongest match available and leaves no ambiguity at all — and
returned a clean **"no results found"** for Taunton Aesthetics and CCS Aesthetics, which is a real
answer rather than a gap. The names are distinctive enough that the alphabetical-ranking problem
never appeared.

**CQC, HIS, HIW and the ICO register are STILL untried, and there are now three clinics that need
them.** Taunton Aesthetics and CCS Aesthetics returned nothing on Companies House under any name,
and The Aesthetics Clinic cannot be searched by registered office because it publishes no town at
all. All three are otherwise good, and the CQC provider record naming the legal entity outright is
the obvious next call. I ran out of budget before reaching it; it is the cheapest rescue left in
this market.

**Three recorded traps all showed up again, which is the best argument for keeping them written
down.** A company name inside a **Fresha booking URL slug** (Secret Skin Aesthetics) and `Ltd`
inside a **LinkedIn URL slug** (Self Medical Aesthetics) — neither is a publication by the clinic.
A **template placeholder** address, `info@website.com`, printed beside the real one (Snobs
Aesthetics) — not recorded. And a variant of the `tel:` placeholder: Aesthetic Atelier publishes its
address as plain text in a contact block, so it is recordable, while its "Enquire Now" button points
at `http://info@aestheticatelier.co.uk`, a malformed URL nobody ever tested. One new one to add:
**Snobs Aesthetics prints no street address as text at all** — the street appears only in the Fresha
slug, so the address of the premises is as unpublished as a company number in a slug.

**A new rule-out shape worth naming: the dissolved-company answer is a finding, not a blank.**
Young & Beautiful Aesthetics publishes two first-name mailboxes, `kate@` and `mel@`, which reads as
two principals — and PECR excludes a partnership exactly as it excludes a sole trader. The targeted
register search returned four "Young and Beautiful" companies and **all four are dissolved**. That
is not an absence of evidence; it is evidence that no corporate subscriber exists to email.

**Two towns are catchment rather than markets, and the 28 Oct correction applies.** Woking produced
nothing: its only candidate publishes no address and is beauty-led, and the clinics ranking for it
sit in West Byfleet and Weybridge. Northampton produced one row and that clinic is in Wollaston near
Wellingborough. Several other rows are similarly displaced — Health & Aesthetics is in Elstead,
Secret Skin in Hartley Wintney, Mid Yorkshire in Featherstone, Jodie Lauren in Brighouse, Alisha
Louise in Ormskirk, Bodywise and Skin Health in Horwich. **Six of eight sendable rows and most of
the parked ones are in the satellite town, not the named one**, which is how these markets are
actually shaped and is worth building the next query list around.

**Productive towns:** Sunderland (2 rows, 1 sendable), Bolton (2, 1), Exeter (3, 0 — all three fail
the menu), Guildford (3, 1), Huddersfield (2, 1), Telford (2, 1), Portsmouth/Southsea (2, 0).
**Thin but not dry:** Reading, Lincoln, Worcester, Taunton, Wakefield, Chelmsford, Colchester,
Shrewsbury, Basingstoke, Wigan, Northampton — one row each. **Dry:** Woking only, and it is thin
rather than empty — one clinic exists, it just cannot be reached.

**Depth left in this market:** six `robots_disallowed` or erroring sites, every one of them the top
result for its town, which makes this the strongest browser-visit list any UK run has produced —
Linora Aesthetics (Lincoln) and Nicola Haywood (Wakefield) first, since each effectively carries its
town. Then the three clinics awaiting a CQC provider-record check. Then the Bolton, Colchester,
Northampton and Wigan Companies House pages 2 onward, which were never read.

## What this market taught me

**The outer suburbs publish addresses far more readily than the inner metros did — but they do not publish founding years.** Fourteen of the twenty-one clinics whose homepages I could read printed a plain-text mailbox, which is a far better hit rate than the AU inner-metro sweeps recorded, and the homepage carried it almost every time (the brief's "read the homepage footer before `/contact`" held in 13 of 14 cases). But only **two** clinics in the entire sweep published a founding year — Pose Aesthetics ("EST. 2023") and Aesthetica HQ ("Founded in 2025 by Gina and Lo") — and the second of those disqualified itself by printing it. Everything else offers a practitioner's career length ("20+ years nursing", "18+ years combined", "over 10 years") as if it were the business's age. **Must-have 4 is now the binding constraint in this market, not must-have 5.** Three of my five C grades are must-have-4 calls, and the brief should probably say what proxy is acceptable, because "the nurse qualified in 2008" is being used to mean "the clinic has a list" and those are not the same claim.

**Two other things worth writing down.** First, the Melbourne south-east corridor (Berwick–Pakenham–Frankston–Mornington) is the single densest patch of qualifying independents I found — six accepted rows out of nine clinics read — while **the Brisbane bayside (Cleveland, Capalaba, Redland Bay, Victoria Point) is structurally closed**: one query returned ten results and nine were skin-cancer clinics, GP surgeries or bulk-billing practices, which is the "a small market cannot support a pure injectables menu" pattern the NZ sweep found, appearing here in a *large* market because bayside Brisbane's skin business is medical. Do not spend more searches there. Second, **the suburb-stacking technique degrades badly once a query includes more than about four town names plus two modifiers** — my Caboolture/Morayfield/Narangba/Springfield query returned exactly one result (a massage directory), and the Narellan/Camden/Liverpool/Pakenham/Officer query returned mostly UK clinics (Camden Clinic, Liverpool, aesthetic beauty centre) because the US-weighted index matched the town names to the wrong hemisphere. Four suburbs and one modifier worked; six suburbs and three modifiers returned nothing usable twice. That cost me two of my twelve searches and is the reason the Perth outer-ring (Canning Vale, Ellenbrook, Rockingham proper) is still barely covered.

## What this market taught me

**Northwest Arkansas was the find of the run and should have been swept months ago.** Five of the
six clinics I opened there published a readable address — Willow Park, Ziva, Vibrant, VOXY,
Glotologi and Ark Health all gave one up, four of them on the homepage, and three of the four A
grades in my batch came from a corner nobody had touched. The density note in the old file was
right. It is also a small enough market that the same owners recur: Bentonville and Rogers between
them carried a membership, a VIP club, a "VAULT", Boulevard, Jane and Eva Health across six
independents. The catch is that NWA search results are unusually thick with plastic surgeons and
dermatology (Advanced Dermatology & Skin Cancer, Natural State, Taylor, Stubbs), so the blocked
list matters more here than the suburb stacking does.

**The San Antonio suburb ring is the opposite, and the note saying it "has one more pass in it" was
half right.** The pass found plenty of clinics — nine in New Braunfels, Schertz, Helotes, Boerne
and Stone Oak — and almost none of them publishes an address. Eight of my ten total-silence
near-misses are in that ring, and I spent two fetches each on five of them to be sure. The ring is
rich in exactly the signals we grade on (three membership programmes, two genuine banked-credit
schemes, Boulevard, Moxie, Aesthetic Record, two published founding years including a 1975
family-owned clinic) and poor in the one thing we need. **My recommendation: stop emailing into
that ring and hand it to a phone or DM channel.** The single accepted San Antonio row, The Skin
Atelier, published a personal-name mailbox rather than an `info@` — which may be the pattern there:
solo founders publish themselves, teams publish a form.

Two techniques confirmed. **The "stop fetching /contact, fetch the team or about page instead"
rule held, but weakly:** 11 of my 15 addresses came off a homepage and one off a footer, and the
six second fetches I spent on about/team pages produced **zero** new addresses — they settled
ownership (Radiant Heights' owner, Good Medicine's structure, Revify's 2021 founding year), which
is worth having, but a US clinic that hides its address on the homepage hides it everywhere. Treat
the second fetch as an ownership fetch, not an address fetch, and budget accordingly. And **the
suburb-stacked query only works unquoted** — my first San Antonio search stacked six quoted town
names and returned a single result; the same towns unquoted returned ten.

One correction to the standing list: `medspa-sanantonio.com` returned as the only result of a
six-suburb query and looks like a catchment page that owns other clinics' results. Worth blocking.

## What this market taught me

**The inland-California warning in my brief was right, and it bit in the shape predicted.** Of
roughly thirty-two businesses examined, the disqualifications split almost exactly as warned:
plastic-surgery practices with a med spa arm (Bloom, Silhouette, Face n Body, Inland Cosmetic) and
weight-loss or wellness storefronts with injectables bolted on (New Image, Serenity MD, and
EuroPhoria at the edge of it). Screening the menu first saved every one of those a privacy-policy
fetch, and I spent **zero** fetches on a privacy policy all day.

**The binding constraint here is publishing, not supply — and it is worse than any US market in the
log.** Eleven clinics cleared the ICP on profile and failed on the address alone: **nine published
nothing at all, two were Cloudflare-hidden.** That is a 15-accepted-to-11-lost ratio, barely over
1:1, against the roughly 2:1 the log records for Texas, the mid-South and the Upper Midwest. The
independent layer in inland California is genuinely intact and nobody has picked it over — the
accepted rows include two owner-operated Coachella Valley clinics and a 2003-founded Visalia
practice that no sweep has touched. The problem is that these clinics market by phone, text widget
and Instagram. **Ego Defined publishes no email AND no phone number**, on three pages.

**The two best clinics in the whole sweep are both unreachable by email, and both for different
reasons.** Neo Medical Spa (Temecula) has two named co-owners, eight years, and a banked-credit
membership — and a Cloudflare-masked address, which is one browser visit away. Aesthetic Lab
(Modesto, Turlock, Stockton) names its owner-injector outright, runs Zenoti, and publishes nothing
on three pages. The gap between those two is the whole value of the four-way taxonomy: one is a
five-minute job for Jess, the other needs a phone call.

**`/contact` is dead in the US for the fifth consecutive sweep, and I can now put a number on it.**
I spent five contact-page fetches (Neo, Aesthetic Lab, Cox, Desert Med, Health & Beauty). They
produced **one** address, and that one was corroborated on the homepage anyway — so the net yield
of five contact-page fetches was **zero addresses the homepage would not have given**. Of fifteen
accepted rows, thirteen addresses came off a homepage or footer and two off an About page. The
team page earned its keep differently, exactly as the 29 Oct note predicted: it produced no
addresses at all, but it settled ownership for Aesthetic Lab, Alyne, Revay and Eleven Aesthetics,
and must-have 3 was the hardest must-have in this market.

**"Established" is the binding filter here, not scale and not cash-pay.** Only **two of fifteen**
accepted rows published a real founding year — ABLC Visalia ("Since Opening in 2003") and, in the
near-misses, Desert Med Aesthetics (founded 2004). Thirteen rows say "established not verified" or
"established inferred" out loud, and the proxies I used are review counts (Rio Glow's 122), dated
awards (Jade MD's 2025 chamber award), footer copyrights (The Retreat RX's 2022) and team size
(Alyne's eleven staff). **The career-tenure trap caught four clinics** — Belle Ame's "20+ years of
combined experience", Desert Glow's "over 20 years", The Retreat RX's "over 10 years in
aesthetics" and Alyne's "business owners in Tracy for over 20 years" — and not one of them is the
clinic's trading history. Every one is flagged in its row.

**A sixth sweep with zero consent refusals.** Fifteen accepted clinics plus seventeen examined,
and not one site carries any statement refusing unsolicited commercial email. Several carry SMS
consent language with STOP instructions and say nothing about email at all.

**Two town-level findings.** Visalia was the surprise of the sweep: three accepted rows from one
town of about 140,000, which is more than Fresno, Stockton, Modesto and Bakersfield produced
between them. And the **northern valley badly underperformed the inland south** — six northern
towns gave two rows (Alyne in Tracy, LAC in Merced) against nine from the inland south, despite
the northern valley being the larger and more obvious target. If one half of this market gets a
second pass, it should be Stockton, Modesto, Lodi and Turlock with a browser rather than a
fetcher, because four of the five clinics lost there are lost to publishing and two of them are
the best clinics in their towns.

**Depth left, honestly marked.** **Genuinely unswept:** Manteca, Hanford and Clovis produced no
clinic domain of their own on any query — each appeared only as somebody else's service-area page,
which the log's catchment rule says is a lead about a metro and not about the town, so treat them
as unresolved rather than as depth. **Murrieta** was never queried on its own and is covered only
as Temecula's catchment — it is the clearest unworked gap. **Fowler** was not reached at all.
Bakersfield and Fresno are now worked to about one row each across two sweeps and should be left
alone. I stopped on budget with four Bakersfield-area names unopened (Brilyn Medical Health,
Empire Aesthetic Center) and Murrieta untouched — this is the first sweep in five to stop on
budget rather than on supply, which is itself the finding: **inland California has more supply than
the budget could work.**


# UK near-misses and rule-outs — round three — 1 November 2026

Towns worked: Ilkley, Harrogate, Altrincham, Stockport (Hazel Grove and Heaton Moor), Chester,
Solihull, Sutton Coldfield, Loughborough, Tunbridge Wells, Crowborough, Bury St Edmunds, Ayr,
Perth, Stirling, plus Newark-on-Trent and Clowne which arrived as catchment displacement.
ICP v2 under the UK corporate-subscriber screen (must-have 8). Rows went to `uk-round3.json`;
everything below either cannot be emailed or was ruled out on the standard.

Run on **10 WebSearch calls and 45 WebFetch calls** — the fetch cap was reached exactly, with two
searches left unspent so the other three workers were not starved. **No fetched page attempted to
steer the extraction this run**; every one of the twenty site fetches was asked to treat page text
as data and all twenty reported clean.

I grepped `clinic-pipeline.csv` and `near-misses.md` for every name before spending a fetch.
**No duplicate reached the JSON.** One clinic below — Harrogate Aesthetics — is already in
`near-misses.md` from an earlier pass, and is repeated here only because this run found something
decisive that the earlier entry does not have.

## The regulator rescue route — attempted, and it is still blocked

This was one of my instructions and it did not work, so record the result rather than the intent.

- **CQC returns `client_error` to a fetch.** A search found the exact location record I wanted —
  `https://www.cqc.org.uk/location/1-26035043607`, "Currentbody Skin: The Clinic (Cheshire)" — and
  the fetch of that page failed outright with nothing retrieved. One fetch spent, nothing learned
  beyond the failure mode.
- **The ICO public register cannot be queried by URL at all.** Its search at
  `https://ico.org.uk/ESDWebPages/Search` is a POST form; individual entries are reachable
  (`/ESDWebPages/Entry/ZB065384` and similar surfaced in search results) but **only if you already
  know the registration number**, which is precisely what we are trying to find. There is no
  fetchable search-by-name URL.
- **So the untried rescue route is still untried, and it is not a budget problem — it is a tooling
  problem.** CQC, HIS, HIW and the ICO all need a **browser**, not another fetch. The three clinics
  from 29 October waiting on this (Taunton Aesthetics, CCS Aesthetics, The Aesthetics Clinic) are
  still waiting, and **no amount of worker fetch budget will clear them.** Put them on Jess's
  browser list beside the `robots_disallowed` sites. Worth noting in the brief so the next worker
  does not spend the same two fetches discovering the same thing.

## Towns assigned that I never reached

Said plainly, because the next worker should start here rather than re-derive it: **York, Wilmslow,
Huddersfield, Leamington Spa, Derby proper, Winchester, Salisbury, Cambridge, Norwich, Hove,
Sevenoaks and Cowbridge** got no fetch at all. Harrogate, Cambridge, Norwich, Derby, Huddersfield,
Sevenoaks and Leamington Spa already have pipeline rows, so several of those are thin by prior
sweeps rather than unexplored — but York, Wilmslow, Winchester, Salisbury, Hove and Cowbridge are
genuinely untouched.

**And one query failure is worth inheriting.** My stacked search for Winchester + Salisbury +
Sutton Coldfield + Leamington Spa + York, phrased with quoted multi-word town names and six other
terms, returned **exactly one result and it was a directory page**. The brief's advice to stack four
or five towns into one query is sound, but it broke here, and I think the cause is over-constraint:
**quoted multi-word town names plus "nurse prescriber owner email contact" is too many hard
constraints at once.** My productive queries stacked bare town names with two or three soft terms.
That one wasted search cost me the whole southern half of the assignment, so stack the towns, but
keep the rest of the query loose.

---

## What this market taught me

**Round three in Britain is a legal-form problem almost to the exclusion of everything else, and the
number is stark: of 18 rows, only 3 clear every must-have.** Six of the fifteen C grades fail on
**must-have 8 alone** — Ellura, Beyond The Face, MS Aesthetics, Royal Aesthetics, LW Aesthetics and
Elixir Medical Aesthetics are all otherwise fine clinics with readable addresses that PECR will not
let us email. That inverts the 29 October finding, which said cash-pay had overtaken the company
screen as the binding filter. **It had, in the towns swept that day. It has not, in these ones.**
Only three rows failed on the menu this run (Altri Medical, The London Road Clinic, Estheva) against
six on the company test. My reading of why: the previous passes took the larger secondary towns,
where a clinic big enough to need a company is also big enough to bolt on vein and lesion work to
fill the diary. What is left in round three is **smaller and more owner-shaped** — single nurses in
single rooms, often rented inside a host salon — and that is exactly the business that never
incorporates. **The structure that makes a clinic a good prospect on must-have 3 is the structure
that fails it on must-have 8.** That tension is now the central fact about this market, and it will
not improve by sweeping more towns.

**Four of the eighteen rows published their own company identity, and that is a much better rate than
the register gives.** Solihull Aesthetics (13398927), SLS Medical Aesthetics (SC617555), The London
Road Clinic (14362347 plus ICO ZB509067) and The Face Workshop (15026293 plus an ICO and a VAT
number) all print it on their own page — and so does Harrogate Aesthetics, in the near-misses. The
20 October rule says go to the registers first and the clinic's own site last. **That ordering is
right for resolving a clinic you have already decided you want**, but it is worth knowing that one
in four clinics answers must-have 8 on the page you were going to read anyway, for free, in the same
fetch that gets you the address. I folded the company question into my single extraction prompt and
it cost nothing.

**The whole-word and truncation faults both bit, and I can now say which one is actually dangerous.**
Truncation bit three times — Ilkley (192 matches), Bury St Edmunds (22 shown as 20), Stockport (30
shown as 20) — but in two of those the row I needed was on page one anyway, so the fault cost me
nothing but caution. **The dangerous one is the near-miss match.** The Elixir search returned two
companies literally named ELIXIR MEDICAL AESTHETICS and both were Scottish, in Inverness and Elgin,
against a clinic in Loughborough. **An unwary worker records one of those and the row looks
sendable.** Same shape, less tempting, for LW Aesthetics, where the single hit was LW BEAUTY AND
AESTHETICS LIMITED in Wallasey. **A name-and-town mismatch is the trap, not an empty result**, and
the guard is to check the registered office town against the clinic's town every single time, which
costs nothing.

**The clean negative is a real and reportable answer, and three shapes of it showed up.** The
strongest was Ellura: zero results for the name with no status filter at all, which rules out a
dissolved company as well as an active one and is the most complete negative available. Then Beyond
The Face, triangulated three ways — the clinic name, the founder's first name, and the town search
returning its full nine results untruncated. Then MS Aesthetics, where Perth returned its whole set
of seven. **A negative built from a result set you actually saw in full is worth recording as a
finding**, and it is different in kind from LW Aesthetics, where page two of Stockport was never read
and the honest answer is "unresolved". I have marked which is which on every row; the distinction
decides whether one more call is worth making.

**Targeted name searches beat the one-call-per-town search in this round, and the reason is the town
mix.** The ICP prefers one call per town because it answers must-have 8 and must-have 4 for a whole
market at once. That pays when a town has several candidates. These towns had **one each**, so a
town call bought one answer for one fetch and risked truncation, while a name call bought the same
answer with no truncation risk and a cleaner negative. Eight of my eleven register calls were name
calls, and the three town calls (Tunbridge Wells, Bury St Edmunds, Perth) each resolved exactly one
of my clinics plus one near-miss — useful, but not the leverage the ICP describes. **Match the call
shape to the town's density, not to the rule.**

**Nothing graded A, and that is a reporting choice rather than a market finding.** Three rows are
A-shaped — By Jess Aesthetics, Ellura Aesthetics and Beyond The Face each have a named owner-injector,
a dormant-list scheme and (for two of them) a nameable practice system. But the A standard also
requires "busy with real reviews", and **I verified review volume for no clinic in this run** — I
spent every fetch on sites and registers and none on reviews. Grading any of them A would have been
an unevidenced upgrade, so all three sit at B or C with the reason written on the row. If review
checking is worth a fetch each, three rows could move; if it is not, say so and the next worker can
stop treating A as reachable.

**Practice-system detection is nearly always an inference, and the rows say so.** Five of the
eighteen name a CRM only because the booking link resolves to `portal.aestheticnursesoftware.com` or
`bookings.gettimely.com`; **not one of those five pages names its software in the text.** The
inference is sound — those are single-tenant portals — but it is an inference, it is flagged as one
in every `crm_detected` field, and **Aesthetic Nurse Software turning up four times in one eighteen-row
sweep** is itself a finding: it is the default system for the UK solo nurse-injector, the way Pabau
is for the slightly larger clinic. If WILBA ever needs to integrate with one UK system, that is the one.

**Two small-town facts worth keeping.** Ilkley, a town of roughly 15,000, supports **two**
independent aesthetics clinics (The Ilkley Skin Clinic and AW Aesthetics), which is more than the
population floor in the log would predict — so the floor is a floor, not a ceiling. And the catchment
warning paid off twice more: a West Bridgford query returned a clinic in **Newark-on-Trent**, twenty
miles away, through an SEO catchment page, and a Tunbridge Wells query returned one in
**Crowborough** whose own meta description claims Tunbridge Wells while its contact address says
otherwise. **Read the published address against the query town every time**, exactly as the brief says
to read the phone area code in Australia.

## What this market taught me

**Northwest Arkansas is a good market, but the 1 November result was the top of the seam, not the
average.** That run opened six clinics in Bentonville and Rogers and five published an address.
I went into Springdale, Fayetteville and Siloam Springs — the towns that sweep said were untouched —
and got **five published addresses from eleven NWA businesses opened**, with two of the five
(PRISM, Rejuvenated) being exactly the clinics I most wanted. The difference is not that the
outer towns are worse clinics; it is that **Bentonville and Rogers are where the money and the
marketing budgets are, and a clinic with a marketer publishes an address.** NWA is still worth
assigning, but budget it at roughly one address in two, not five in six, and expect Bella Vista,
Centerton and Cave Springs to return nothing of their own — not one search surfaced a clinic sited
in any of the three, which I read as those towns being served from Bentonville and Rogers rather
than having their own practices.

**Eastern and central Oklahoma published far better than Arkansas did, and that was the run's
surprise.** Twelve of the seventeen accepted rows are Oklahoma. The OKC suburb ring in particular
(Edmond, Yukon, Mustang, plus OKC proper) gave six reachable clinics from eight opened — a better
rate than anything in the log except the Bentonville–Rogers seam itself. Tulsa's suburbs split
cleanly: **Broken Arrow, Owasso and Bixby published; Tulsa proper did not.** Both Tulsa-city clinics
I opened (Firm, and Nouveau's neighbour set) were the silent ones, and Firm cost two fetches to
establish that. If anyone goes back, **work the ring and leave the city.**

**The brief's two newest rules both paid, and one of them paid six times.** I spent **five ownership
fetches** onto about, team and story pages. They settled must-have 3 in **five cases out of five**
and produced **zero** new email addresses — Oum, BA Med Spa, ACE, The Treatment Room and Halestorm.
That is now a very large consecutive run of the same result, and it should probably be stated in the
brief as a flat fact rather than as advice: **the second fetch buys ownership, never an address.**
The unquoted four-name cap also held — every one of my ten searches returned ten results, and not
one collapsed into a directory or an out-of-market set.

**The thing I would change about the standard, not the sourcing:** four of the twelve B rows are
B *only* because must-have 4 cannot be read. Nine of the seventeen accepted clinics publish no
founding year at all, and what they publish instead is the practitioner's personal career — "38+
years in healthcare", "over sixteen years of experience", "7+ years medical", "over 13 years in
nursing". Our standard needs clinic tenure and the American med spa web publishes operator tenure.
**Every worker is therefore inferring must-have 4 from a structural proxy** — menu breadth, device
capital, site count — and calling it established. That is worth a decision from Jess rather than
seventeen individually-flagged guesses: either personal tenure plus an operating clinic is accepted
as a tenure proxy, or must-have 4 should be checked against a review-platform date, which is a fetch
nobody currently budgets. Of the four clinics that *did* publish a real founding year — BA Med Spa
(2009), Rejuvenated (2019), Gudgel (2018), SkinFit (2020), Elevate (2018), Ageless (2019) — three
publish no email, which is its own small irony.

**Banked credit clustered, and not where the brief predicts.** The log says the wallet/bank/vault
search is an affluent-suburb technique. I found **three** genuine credit schemes in this run and none
of them was in an affluent suburb: a monthly account credit in **Siloam Springs** (population about
17,000), an auto-drafted spa "wallet" in **Broken Arrow and Jenks**, and a "VIP Savings Account" on a
**dermatology-attached** Fayetteville clinic we cannot use. All three were found by reading the
clinic's own membership copy after landing on the site, never by searching the word — which is
exactly what the brief says the technique is actually for. **Mid-size markets do run banked credit;
they just do not call it a vault.**

**One platform observation worth carrying.** **Moxie** (app.joinmoxie.com) turned up again, in Bixby,
having first appeared in San Antonio on 1 Nov. **Prospyr** (book.prospyrmed.com) appeared for the
first time anywhere in our notes, in Norman. Both are single-tenant practice platforms of the kind
that satisfies the grade-A "nameable practice system" test, and neither is on our list. **Boulevard
was the most common system by a wide margin** — five of seventeen accepted rows plus two near-misses
— and in four of those five it was identifiable only from a `blvd.me` or `dashboard.boulevard.io`
link, never named in page text. The booking link is where to look, exactly as the UK run found for
Aesthetic Nurse Software.

## What this market taught me

**Australia is finished, and the Adelaide coast is the proof.** The clearest single finding of the
run is not a clinic, it is a directory index. I fetched the Yellow Pages "skin treatments & skin
clinics" indexes for **Brighton SA 5048 and Marion SA** on purpose, as the brief's technique 3
prescribes. Both returned the **identical thirty listings**, neither list was local to the suburb
queried, and the contents were **The Body Shop (four times), MAC Cosmetics, L'Occitane, a gym, a
market, two dermatology groups and two skin cancer clinics**. *Not one listing on either index
mentioned cosmetic injectables or a cosmetic nurse.* When a directory that exists to list skin
clinics in a 400,000-person coastal catchment cannot find thirty of them and pads the page with
cosmetics retail, the conclusion is not that my query was wrong. **There is no population of
independent injectables clinics left in Adelaide's western and coastal suburbs.** The corner is
empty, not unswept. Port Adelaide, Semaphore, Henley Beach, Burnside, Brighton and Marion produced,
between eight searches and twenty-two fetches, exactly **two** independents with a readable address
— Skin Afinity in Somerton Park and Skin4U in Glenelg — and the second of those has no injectables.

**Perth's assigned corridors failed for a structural reason, not a search-wording one.** Wanneroo,
Canning Vale, Ellenbrook, Midland and Armadale each produced **one** aesthetics candidate, and in
three of the five that candidate **also sells skin cancer checks or minor surgery** (West Coast Skin
in Wanneroo, Skin Hub in Canning Vale) or is a beauty salon with a visiting nurse (The Beauté
Collective in Midland). This is the brief's own New Zealand lesson repeating: *an outer suburb
cannot support a pure injectables menu*, so the clinics that exist there survive by adding
Medicare-billed work, which fails must-have 2. **Screening the menu first saved four privacy-policy
fetches** and is now confirmed in a second market.

**Three of my twelve searches were destroyed by place-name collisions, and the area-code rule caught
all three.** `Armadale Gosnells Kelmscott Thornlie ... WA` returned **Washington State** — "WA" is
the collision, so never put the bare state abbreviation in a query with small-town names. `Midland
Ellenbrook Bassendean Guildford` returned **Midland Ontario** (area code 705), **Midland Texas**,
and **Guildford Surrey** — four towns, three countries, one query. The fix that worked was spelling
out "Perth WA" or "Adelaide" *and* keeping the stack to four names plus two modifiers; the
unquoted-and-short rule held up, but **it does not protect against a name that exists in three
countries.** Add that to the rule: prefer suburb names that are unique in the English-speaking
world (Wanneroo, Ellenbrook, Semaphore) over ones that are not (Midland, Brighton, Armadale,
Richmond, Guildford).

**The device-maker locator technique has lost its best Australian source.**
`deviceconsulting.com.au/clinic-locator` — the one locator that surfaced for this market — returns a
**client error** and no content on any path. Of the eight locators the brief lists, Aesthetics Rx,
Cosmeceutical Solutions and dermaviduals render client-side, ZO is robots-disallowed, and this one
is now simply broken. **The technique still has the best yield per fetch where a static locator
exists, but Australia no longer has one — do not budget fetches for it here again.**

**Two Australian clinic sites in one run were serving injected content, which is new.** Skin4U's page
source contains **PHP that logs a visitor in as an administrator** on certain URL paths plus casino
links, and ORO Aesthetics serves casino links and Polish-language blocks inside the clinic's own
content. Neither tried to steer what I recorded, so this is not the Louisville case; it is
compromised WordPress. But it is a reason to **read the `notes` field before emailing either** — a
mailbox on a compromised host may be unattended or itself compromised — and a sixth thing that looks
like clinic content and is not.

**The consent screen still has not disqualified a single Australian clinic.** That is now five
sweeps and, on this run, four privacy policies read in full (Skin Afinity, Jennifer Carly, Luum,
and About Face's pages). Every one of them either says nothing about unsolicited email or says the
**opposite** — Luum's policy volunteers that it may send direct marketing and names its CRM
provider. It remains a recording cost, not a filter, and leaving it to last was right. **Not
guessing `/privacy-policy` paths also worked**: four of five policy links I used were read off a
page I had already fetched and all four resolved; the fifth, Mira Clinic's, was **robots-disallowed**,
so I recorded the no-notice finding for the page I actually read and said which page that was,
rather than claiming a screen I had not completed.

**My verdict: stop assigning Australia.** Eight rows, none of them A, and five of the eight sit
*outside* the corners I was sent to (Gawler, West Perth, Joondalup, Highett) because the corners
themselves were bare. The remaining Australian value is not in sourcing at all — it is the
**browser-visit list**: Fika Clinic's obfuscated mailbox, Peninsula Skin Co's robots block, and
above all the two Fulham Gardens injectors with no findable website. That is twenty minutes of
Jess's own browsing, not another sourcing run.

## What this market taught us

**The southeast publishes an address more readily than the US average, and the obfuscation
problem is small here.** Twenty-nine clinics were examined closely and seventeen gave a
verbatim address, which is a far better rate than the "total silence is the commonest US
failure" note in the brief would predict. Only three of the twelve unreachable ones were
Cloudflare-hidden; the rest simply publish nothing, so this is a phone market more than a
browser market. The one address pattern worth recording is **how often it is a gmail**: five
of the seventeen (Colonial, Mela, Destin, Oak and Glow, Beauty Queens) publish a free mailbox
rather than one on their own domain, which is a much higher mismatch rate than the roughly one
in five seen on 21 Oct, and a hint that these are small operations where the owner reads her
own mail — good for us, but it means a bounce is likelier and must be read as a bounce.

**The brief's two measured corrections both held exactly.** Unquoted four-town stacks with two
modifiers returned ten usable results every time, across six different stacks, and not one
collapsed into a directory or the wrong region. And **no `/contact` was fetched at all**: every
one of the seventeen addresses came off a homepage, an About page or a memberships-page footer,
which now makes it 76 in a row. The ownership-fetch rule held too but is worth sharpening —
**the single second fetch onto a team or About page settled ownership three times out of three
and produced zero new addresses**, exactly as predicted. The Injectory is the clean case: the
homepage gave the address and a testimonial name, and the team page turned a guess into "Bobby-Jo
Lutner, CRNA, owner, launched February 2021".

**The warning about this market was right, and it cost more than the plastic surgeons did.**
Plastic-surgery practices were easy to screen off the menu and never cost a fetch. The real
tax was the **hormone-and-weight-loss middle ground**: eight of the clinics I did fetch carry
GLP-1, HRT or longevity programmes alongside the aesthetic menu, and three of them (Odomí,
MedSpa 501, Dr Addison) are genuinely arguable rather than clear. I accepted all three with the
doubt written into `notes` rather than smoothed over, because the aesthetic menus are full and
listed first, but **Dr Addison Aesthetics is the one to re-screen before sending** — her second
board is Obesity Medicine, and a practice whose lapsed list is mostly weight-management patients
is not a practice our offer works on.

**Two structural things to carry forward.** First, **Lost Key Med Spa is the case for always
reading the phone before the town**: it publishes a toll-free 833 number and no street address,
so the area-code check the brief mandates simply could not be run, and the only evidence for
"Pensacola" is a meta description. That failure mode is new to this log — not a wrong town, but
an **uncheckable** one. Second, **Ageless Skin Rejuvenation found a fifth look-alike address**:
not Cloudflare, not a builder placeholder, not a QR code and not the clinic's own Open Graph
tag, but **the marketing agency's mailbox served in a `twitter:data1` meta tag**. It reads like
a published address to anything scraping metadata and it belongs to a third party, so it is
arguably worse than a placeholder. Worth adding to the four in both the brief and ICP.

**Coverage left behind.** The search budget died before Norfolk proper, Newport News and Suffolk
got a dedicated stack — all three were only ever reached as the third or fourth name in someone
else's query, and Norfolk produced no independent clinic domain of its own at all. Mount Pleasant
SC and Pooler GA were likewise never searched directly. Savannah, Pensacola, Greenville SC and
Chapel Hill are now properly covered; **Norfolk and Newport News are still at zero and should be
the first stack of the next run.**

## What this market taught me

**Las Vegas is the worst publishing market in the entire log, and it is not close.** I examined
**twenty-two Nevada businesses** and got **five readable addresses** — and two of those five
(Aethereal, Blanqa) are graded C for being too new to have a list, and one (The Treatment) is a
five-site group. **Nevada produced exactly three usable rows: Tru Beauty, Glamour Me and Abrams,
plus Center for Aesthetic Medicine off a privacy policy.** Against yesterday's inland-California
ratio of fifteen accepted to eleven lost — which the log already called the worst in the file —
Nevada is roughly **4 accepted to 11 unreachable**, so **inland California is now the second-worst
market and Las Vegas is the worst.** The texture is different too: inland California clinics market
by phone, text widget and Instagram, whereas the Las Vegas ones are **conspicuously well-built sites
with Zenoti, Mangomint, Vagaro and PatientNow behind them that simply never print a mailbox.** These
are not scrappy operations hiding; they are funded operations that treat the phone and the booking
widget as the only front door. **The practical consequence: Las Vegas needs a phone or Instagram-DM
route, not an email route**, and the decision the 24 Sep sweep asked for about non-email channels is
now overdue rather than optional.

**The privacy policy was the single highest-yield fetch of the day, and the ICP is right about it.**
Two of my sixteen rows exist only because of it — **Liquid Beauty** (`info@liquidbeauty.com`, in a
"you may contact us regarding this policy" clause, where the homepage published nothing) and **Center
for Aesthetic Medicine** (`info@camhplv.com`, printed three times on the policy page). Both are among
my four best rows. Two policy fetches, two addresses, in a market where thirty-odd homepage and About
fetches produced fourteen. **In a silent market, go to the privacy policy early rather than last.**
That inverts what the brief currently implies for the US, where the policy is framed as a last resort
and the consent screen as a mere recording cost.

**`/contact` is dead in the US for the sixth consecutive sweep, and I only broke the rule once and
only legitimately.** I spent exactly one `/contact` fetch, on ReNew Medical Aesthetics in Visalia,
**because no homepage URL for that domain ever appeared in a search result** — so it was the *first*
fetch on the domain, not a second one chasing an address the homepage had withheld. It produced an
address. **That is worth writing into the brief as the one exception:** the rule is about not
re-asking a page that already refused, so `/contact` as a first and only fetch on a domain whose
homepage never surfaced is a different thing and it works.

**Two mismatched mailbox domains in sixteen rows, both on good clinics.** `reception@trubeautymedspa.com`
on `trubeautybytrevor.com`, and `info@camhplv.com` on `centerforaestheticmedicine.com`. Recorded
exactly as printed, per the ICP, and flagged on both rows so a bounce reads as a bounce. Also two
rows where the same mailbox is printed with different capitalisation in the contact block and the
footer (Beauty Within, ReNew) — recorded in the contact-block form.

**Suburb-stacked unquoted queries worked, and the cap is real.** Every query I ran was unquoted and
held to four town names plus two modifiers, and none collapsed into an unrelated directory the way
the 1 Nov over-long stacks did. Two things degraded results anyway: **gift-card reseller domains**
(giftly, quickgifts) which own "gift cards" plus a suburb name, and **"email"/"contact" as a
modifier**, which pulled in a window-coverings company and a drug-rehab centre. Better modifiers in
a silent market are **"owner", "founder", "RN injector", "rewards"** — my best single query of the
day was "independent medical spa injectables founded owner rewards program", which returned ten
fresh clinic domains and no directories at all.

**"Established" is the binding filter here too, and worse than yesterday.** Only **two of sixteen**
rows publish a real trading history read off the page — Liquid Beauty ("founded 2016", 2,472+
reviews) and Synergy Laser ("for 22 years") — with Beauty Within's "June 2022" a third but marginal.
The career-tenure trap caught **five** clinics: Inner Beauty's "35 years as a Registered Nurse",
Glamour Me's "9+ Years In Medical" (ambiguous and flagged as such), Naturalness's "21+ years in
nursing", Summerlin Med Spa's "Fifteen Years in Nursing" and Verity's "over five years". Not one is
a founding date and every one is flagged in its row.

**The gaps I was sent to close, honestly marked.** **Closed:** Murrieta (two rows — Naturalness
accepted, Lucali unreachable — it was the best of the five gap towns), **Clovis** (Inner Beauty & Skin,
the first Clovis clinic of its own any sweep has found; Aesthetic Club unresolved behind robots),
**Manteca** (Beauty Within, likewise the first), **Lake Elsinore/Menifee/Wildomar** (resolved as
**catchment, not markets** — every result was a Temecula or Murrieta clinic serving them, or a
surgical practice, and Synergy Laser is the row that covers them). **Still open:** **Hanford,
Lemoore and Selma** produced no clinic domain of their own on a dedicated query — only Visalia and
Fresno practices ranking into them, which the log's catchment rule says is a lead about Visalia, not
about Hanford. **Fowler was not reached at all for the second day running** and I now doubt there is
anything there: it is a town of about 5,500 and two targeted queries never surfaced a single
business. **Anthem and Seven Hills** are the same — they appear only as Henderson clinics' catchment
copy (Aethereal names both), and I would stop treating them as separate markets. **Boulder City has
exactly one aesthetics business** (Refresh MD) and should be marked thin, not unswept.

the Upstate. Nothing goes on the browser-visit list from this run.

## Group 3 — Defeated the fetch

**Nothing in this group either.** No Cloudflare, no robots refusals, no client-side-rendered shells
and no site-side errors across twenty-nine businesses opened. Every fetch returned readable content.
After 2 Nov lost six of seventeen businesses to these modes, that is a striking difference and I do
not have an explanation for it beyond market composition — these are WordPress-and-Squarespace towns.

One technique failure to record instead, so nobody repeats it:
- **`portraitcare.com/directory/.../sapulpa/` is not a directory index.** It surfaced looking like one
  and I fetched it on purpose as a source of names, per the brief's technique 3. It is a **vendor
  marketing page**: six clinic logos under "Trusted by 1,200+ Clinics Nationwide", no towns, no
  domains, every logo linking to `#`. The six names (Skin Sirens Aesthetics, Skin Sirens LA, Skin &
  Soul Aesthetics, Brittany Aesthetics, Napa Aesthetics, Ethereal Medical Aesthetics) are national
  customers, not Sapulpa clinics. **One fetch wasted. The deliberate-directory-fetch technique needs
  the site to be an actual directory — check the result page is a listing before spending the fetch.**

## What these markets taught me

**Privacy-policy-first is now the strongest single technique I have, and it is not only for quiet
markets.** Six of the twenty-two accepted addresses came off a privacy policy that was absent from
the homepage: Numa Spa, Mariposa, Elysian, Inject Tulsa, and the corroborating reads on Soul Tulsa
and Venus. Four homepage-plus-policy pairs returned nothing at all. On yesterday's framing I would
have read the menu first and left the policy till last in Oklahoma, which published well — and I
would have lost four of those six. The better rule may be simpler than the conditional one: **when a
homepage has no mailbox, the privacy policy is the next fetch, always, before the About page and
instead of `/contact`.** The About-page-as-ownership-fetch rule held perfectly again — four About or
team fetches, zero new addresses, ownership settled every time.

**Tulsa city proper was the surprise, and it reverses 2 Nov's conclusion.** That sweep found "Tulsa's
ring published; Tulsa proper did not" and both Tulsa-city clinics it opened were unreachable. Tulsa
city gave me **eight accepted rows out of nine opened** — Align 918, Glow Medical, Core Medicine, HE
Med Spa, Clinical Aesthetics, Luminate, Inject Tulsa and Soul. The difference was the query, not the
town: "Tulsa Sand Springs Sapulpa Claremore" and "Tulsa midtown Brookside Cherry Street" reached
clinics that "Tulsa med spa" never surfaces. **Naming the neighbourhoods inside a city works the way
naming suburbs around one does** — Brookside and Cherry Street alone produced five new domains. That
is a technique I had not seen written down and it is worth adding to the brief.

**Coastal Virginia is genuinely thin, and the 2 Nov A-rate was a small-sample artefact.** Norfolk,
Newport News, Hampton, Yorktown, Smithfield, Portsmouth and Suffolk — seven towns, five queries,
**five accepted rows and not one A**. Norfolk proper has now had four queries across two sweeps and
has produced exactly one reachable independent (Medical Aesthetics of Virginia, and only off a
contact page fetched under the no-homepage exception). What Hampton Roads actually has is
dermatology groups, plastic-surgery practices and a New Hampshire chain's town pages; the
independents that exist mostly publish a phone number and nothing else. **I would call the Virginia
coast finished.** Oklahoma is the opposite: fifteen rows from this run on top of twelve from 2 Nov,
and OKC's suburb ring still has Moore, Midwest City, Del City and Choctaw producing nothing of their
own, which suggests those towns' clinics are the OKC-proper ones under service-area pages.

**Two of the five address look-alikes turned up, and one new near-miss of a trap.** HE Med Spa prints
`info@medicaldirectorco.com` — a third-party medical-director service's mailbox, visible in page
text, on a page where the clinic's own Gmail address also appears. It is not a meta-tag case, so the
brief's fifth look-alike does not quite cover it: **a clinic can publish a vendor's working mailbox
in plain text.** The domain check is what caught it. And Luminate publishes
`hello@luminate.sprucecare.com`, a messaging vendor's subdomain issued to the clinic — recorded,
because it is clinic-named and in visible text, but it is the same shape of question. **Four of
twenty-two accepted addresses sit on a domain other than the website's** (cayennebeauty.com,
elysianokc.com, caotulsa.com, luminate.sprucecare.com), plus one on icloud.com — so the mismatch
rate here is about a quarter, close to the 21 Oct Australian figure. None was corrected.

**No page tried to steer the fetch.** Twenty-nine businesses opened, sixty-one fetches, and nothing
read as instructions, nothing carried injected content, and no source looked compromised. Every
fetch ran with the data-not-instructions prompt in place regardless.

# 4 November 2026 — the UK southern half, the California Central Valley remainder, and Canada round four (Greater Toronto suburbs, Ottawa, Vancouver Island)

Three sweeps, 51 accepted rows (ids 933-983, 5 A / 22 B / 24 C). The three market reports follow
in the order they came back.

# UK southern half — near-misses and rule-outs — 4 November 2026

Market: the southern half of the UK, towns not yet swept. London deliberately avoided throughout.
ICP v2 applied, with the UK corporate-subscriber screen (must-have 8) as the binding filter.
Accepted rows went to `uk-south.json`: **21 rows, 2 A / 5 B / 14 C**.

**Budget: 14 of 16 searches and 58 of 70 fetches.** I stopped on judgement rather than budget — the
marginal fetch had started buying parked C rows instead of sendable ones. Of the 58 fetches,
**23 were Companies House calls** and 35 were clinic pages (3 of those failed outright, 1 was a
redirect notice), giving roughly 31 successful page reads across **27 distinct businesses**.

**No fetched page attempted to steer the extraction.** Every site fetch carried an instruction to
treat page text as data and ignore anything resembling a direction, and all of them reported clean.
One page (Penarth Aesthetic Clinic's contact page) carried a block of stuffed keyword phrases,
which the extractor correctly read as SEO filler rather than instructions.

## Skipped before any fetch, via the grep

I grepped `clinic-pipeline.csv` and `near-misses.md` for every clinic name and every domain before
spending a fetch. **No duplicate reached the JSON.** Three were caught:

- **Innersense Aesthetics** (York and Wetherby) — already **pipeline row 425, grade A**. It is the
  reason York was not virgin ground, and it is the best clinic in that town.
- **Dawn Clinic** (Penarth, Cardiff) — already **pipeline row 438, grade C**. It was the top result
  on my first Welsh query, so the grep saved a fetch immediately.
- **`whealthclinic.co.uk`** (York) — already recorded in `near-misses.md` (line ~1638) as a domain
  that redirects to another company, which the ICP disqualifies. It was result 4 on my York query.

The grep also paid off in an unexpected direction: **`maesthetics.co.uk` (Salisbury) matched nine
rows in the CSV and I nearly treated it as covered.** All nine were `hdmaesthetics.co.uk` in Hull
and other substring collisions. **A substring grep hit is not a duplicate — check the whole domain
before skipping a clinic**, or the grep that is meant to save fetches will quietly cost rows.

## What this market taught me

**The headline, and it beats the floor I was given.** The brief set expectations at "about three
sendable rows from eighteen researched" and told me not to pad. **I researched 27 businesses and
got 7 sendable rows — 2 A and 5 B — plus 14 parked C rows, every one with its failing must-have
named by number.** Must-have 8 was satisfied on **10 of the 21 rows**. So PECR removed about half
this market, not nearly all of it. The structural ceiling is real but it is lower than the standing
estimate, and the reason is in the next two paragraphs.

**Four of twenty-one clinics answered must-have 8 on their own page, for free, in the same fetch
that got me the address** — KM Aesthetics ("KM Aesthetics (South Wales) Ltd… no. 12285892"), EIRA
Clinics ("a trading name of Kate Bell Ltd", 14719551), Be Aesthetic Clinic ("company number
09756418") and Aesthetics by Dr Katherine ("Aesthetics By Dr Katherine Limited… Registered in
England & Wales", named but **not numbered**). That is the same one-in-four rate the 1 Nov worker
measured, independently reproduced, and it confirms their recommendation: **fold the company
question into the single extraction prompt.** It costs nothing and it produced the run's best row.
One refinement on top of theirs: **a company *name* with no number is still a must-have 8 pass**
(the ICP asks for "Ltd", "Limited" or a company number — any one of them), and I nearly spent a
register call confirming something the footer had already answered.

**NEW COMPANIES HOUSE FAULT, and I rate it alongside the near-miss trap. `registeredOfficeAddress`
matches street names, not just towns.** Searching `aesthetics` + `Salisbury` returned twenty
companies of which **six were not in Salisbury at all** — they sat on a Salisbury Road, Salisbury
Avenue or Salisbury Place in Slough, Pudsey, Rotherham, Hounslow, Market Rasen and Blandford Forum.
Worse, `cosmetic` + `Salisbury` returned **exactly one** company and it was in **Hounslow**, on
Salisbury Road. This compounds the truncation fault rather than sitting beside it: the filter pads
the result set with out-of-town companies, which then push the genuine local ones off the 20-row
page. **Remedy: read the town inside every returned address before believing it, and never treat a
20-result page as complete.** A worker who trusts the address filter will report a clean negative
for a town they never actually saw.

**The near-miss trap fired four times in one run — more than any previous sweep — and three of the
four were *exact* name matches.** AESTHETICS SUITE LTD (Nottingham, dissolved) against The
Aesthetics Suite in Wilmslow; KS AESTHETICS LTD (active, Oct 2025) against K S Aesthetics
Salisbury; FACE TO FACE SKINCARE AND AESTHETICS CLINIC LIMITED (dissolved) against Face to Face
Skincare in Haywards Heath; JB COSMETIC DENTURES LTD (Bath) against JB Cosmetic in Wales. Each one
would have read as a pass. **And there is a sub-pattern worth adding to the brief: two of the four
were registered at London mass-registration service addresses — 71-75 Shelton Street, Covent
Garden, and 1 Quality Court, Chancery Lane.** Those addresses are a tell in themselves. A
single-nurse clinic in Salisbury does not register its company in Covent Garden. **Treat a London
service address on a provincial clinic's name match as a near-miss until something ties them
together.** The guard that worked every time, as the ICP says, is checking the registered office
town against the clinic's town — and the strongest passes were the four rows where the registered
office was **byte-identical to the clinic's published street address** (Flamingo, The Medical
Aesthetic Clinic, Age Repair, Facial Aesthetics Centre).

**A CORRECTION TO THE 3 NOV PRIVACY-POLICY RULE, offered as a market difference rather than a
refutation.** The rule says: no mailbox on the homepage, the policy is the next fetch, unconditional.
**In Britain it produced nothing.** I spent exactly one policy fetch as an address-and-company fetch
(The Aesthetics Suite) and it returned a mailbox I already had from the homepage, **no company
identity, no company number, no ICO number, no VAT number and no named data controller** — the
reverse of what the rule predicts. Meanwhile the homepage or its footer gave me the address on
**20 of the 22 sites that published one at all**. And the rule frequently has nothing to act on:
**six of the clinics I opened have no privacy policy page in existence** — Ros Norton, Aesthetics by
Debbie, Face to Face Skincare, Winchester Facial Aesthetics, Facial Aesthetics Centre, and Be
Aesthetic Clinic, which links a cancellation policy and T&Cs instead. The 3 Nov evidence was six
addresses off Oklahoma policies; the underlying logic (a policy must name a contact for data
requests) depends on the clinic having written one. **The UK equivalent of the policy fetch is the
Companies House call**: it is where the thing Britain actually withholds — legal identity — is kept,
and 23 of my 58 fetches went there and resolved must-have 8 for ten rows. Keep the rule for the US;
in the UK, go to the register instead.

**THE RULE I THINK IS WRONG, and it cost this run three clinics. Must-have 2's vein clause is
miscalibrated for Britain.** Must-have 2 is a *cash-pay* test. The rule "vein work is a fail" was
learned in Australia, where vein work attracts a Medicare rebate and is therefore a genuine proxy
for insurance billing. **In the UK, cosmetic thread-vein removal — IPL or sclerotherapy — is never
NHS- or insurance-funded. It is pure private cash-pay.** Applied mechanically, the clause removed
**Sharp Fix Aesthetics** (Lymington — whose must-have 8 is *already satisfied* with an exact-name
active company, 97 Google reviews, two sites and a named founder; the only blemish on it is one
line reading "Thread Vein Removal – IPL"), **Sci-U Clinic** and **NJH Aesthetics** — and it removed
Harrogate Aesthetics on 1 Nov for the same reason. I applied the rule as written rather than
reinterpreting the standard mid-run, and graded all three C with must-have 2 named so the call is
reversible in seconds. **Proposal for Jess: in the UK, narrow the vein clause to venous disease and
varicose work — which does imply a vascular or insurance-adjacent practice — and let cosmetic IPL
thread veins pass.** Sharp Fix becomes a B the moment that is decided, with no further research.
Note the two are not equivalent: Sci-U and NJH list **sclerotherapy** outright, which is the firmer
form of the fail, while Sharp Fix lists only IPL. If the clause is narrowed, rescue Sharp Fix first.

**A PRACTICE-SYSTEM FINDING THAT IS COSTING US GRADE-A ROWS RIGHT NOW.**
`portal.aestheticnursesoftware.com` — **Aesthetic Nurse Software** — appeared on **seven** of the
clinics I opened: The Aesthetics Suite (Wilmslow), Aesthetics by Debbie (Haywards Heath), The
Flamingo Clinic (Shoreham), Penarth Aesthetic Clinic, JB Cosmetic (Wales), Jennifer Siàn (Wimborne)
and NJH Aesthetics (Lincoln). By contrast Timely, Fresha, Cliniko and Pabau each appeared **once**.
**It is not on the ICP's nameable-system list**, which means a worker reading that list literally
records "no practice system" for the single commonest platform in the British nurse-led segment and
downgrades every one of those clinics from A to B. Two more British systems also surfaced and are
also absent from the list: **facesconsent.com** (Faces Consent) and **aesthetidocs.app**, plus
Shortcuts Software, Salonized, Setmore, Acuity and Vagaro at the salon end. **Recommendation: add
Aesthetic Nurse Software, Faces Consent and Aesthetidocs to the grade-A nameable-system list.**

**The Tulsa and twitter:data1 mailbox rules both got live confirmation in the same run, and the
brief is right on both.** Marlow Skin Clinic prints its parent **dental group's** mailbox,
`hello@dentopediagroup.com`, in plain visible footer text — prominent, working, wrong domain. NJH
Aesthetics serves `hello@veryvivid.co.uk`, its **web developer's** mailbox, in a `twitter:data1`
tag — the exact tag the brief names. Neither was recorded. **Whose domain it is really is the only
test**, and a worker checking the domain of every address catches both in seconds.

**Street names inside a town work the way district names inside a city do — second independent
confirmation of the 3 Nov neighbourhood finding.** My first Hove query (Portslade, Kemptown,
Rottingdean) returned NHS surgeries, dentists, pharmacies and directories and **not one Hove clinic
on its own domain**. The second query named Hove's two shopping streets — **"Church Road Western
Road"** — and returned **EIRA Clinics**, which is now a grade-B row at a Hove address with a company
number printed on its own page. On the first query's evidence I would have written Hove off.
**Before writing a town off, spend one query on the names of its shopping streets.**

**A town with no clinic is not a dry hole if a neighbouring clinic claims it.** Cowbridge has no
aesthetics clinic on its own domain at all — the queries returned dentists, NHS practices,
podiatrists and a chiropodist directory. But stacking Cowbridge with Llantwit Major, Bridgend and
Barry surfaced **KM Aesthetics** in Pencoed, which names Cowbridge in its own "areas we serve" list
and is **the best row in this run** (grade A, company number on its own page, 535 reviews, NMC PIN
published, gift vouchers and a mailing list). Record Cowbridge as *covered by catchment*, not as dry.

**Where the UK actually publishes, measured.** Of 27 businesses opened, **22 published a readable
address on their own domain** (81%) — far better than Nevada's 5-of-22 and comparable to New
Zealand. The failures were two robots refusals, one site-side error, two total silences and one
builder placeholder. **Britain publishes its mailbox freely and withholds its legal identity**,
which is the precise inverse of the US, where the fit is easy and the address is everything. It also
means the two UK screens are **not** anti-correlated, confirming the 22 Oct correction: of the ten
rows that answered must-have 8, every single one also had a readable address.

**On the 1 Nov "smaller and more owner-shaped means never incorporates" theory — partly right, and
the refinement is about trading history, not legal form.** Six of my fourteen C rows fail on
must-have 8, which is the same shape the 1 Nov worker found. But **three fail on must-have 4
instead** (Aesthetics by Dr Katherine, started 2024; Aesthetics by Debbie, incorporated April 2024;
and Trudy Mills, incorporated seven weeks ago and ruled out from the register). What the register
shows, now that I have twenty-odd incorporation dates in front of me, is that **the British
owner-injector segment is young**: of the companies I resolved, the median incorporation is around
2021. The clinics old enough to have a 300+ lapsed list — The Medical Aesthetic Clinic (2004),
Springwell (2014), Be Aesthetic (2015), Flamingo (2018), KM (2019) — are also, without exception,
the ones that incorporated. **Age and incorporation go together here.** So the practical filter is
not "does it have a company" but "is it old enough to have a list", and the register answers both
questions in one call. That is a happier conclusion than the 1 Nov one: the tension is not between
must-have 3 and must-have 8, it is simply that half this market is too new.

**Budget honesty.** 14 of 16 searches and 58 of 70 fetches. I stopped with 12 fetches and 2 searches
in hand because the marginal fetch had stopped producing sendable rows — the last six site fetches
produced one B row (Springwell), two C rows and three rule-outs. Two searches were left unspent so
parallel workers were not starved. **Nothing in this run was cut short by budget**; the binding
constraint was the supply of clinics old enough to qualify.

# California Central Valley remainder — near misses and rule-outs — 4 November 2026

**Market assigned:** the Central Valley remainder — **Hanford, Lemoore, Selma**, plus Visalia's and
Fresno's outer ring where anything surfaced that was not already in our files. Central Fresno and
Bakersfield were off-limits as already worked.

Qualified against ICP v2 (16 Oct 2026). No regional screen applies to the US beyond must-have 5,
and no site read today carried any statement refusing unsolicited commercial email (checked on the
four privacy policies and two terms pages I read: thespaatfgv.com, mystiquemedicalspa.com,
savageserenityspa.com, excellencemedicalspa.com/terms-of-use, plus the policy links found but not
needed on amafresno.com and cyruscosmeticsfresno.net).

**Accepted rows: 7** — 0 A / 3 B / 4 C — in `central-valley.json`.
**Spent: 16 WebSearch of 16 (exhausted), 43 WebFetch of 70.** I stopped on **searches**, not fetches,
and not on supply in the sense that matters: there was nothing left to search for. See the closing
section — this market is close to empty rather than merely unreachable.

## What this sweep taught me

**Hanford, Lemoore and Selma do not have an email-reachable aesthetics layer, and the reason is not
search failure.** The 2 Nov worker reported that these towns "produced no clinic domain of their own
on a dedicated query". Two dedicated queries and a local-newspaper fetch later, I can say *why*, and
it is more useful than the gap itself: **the aesthetics businesses in these towns do not own domains.**
Everything that exists there trades on somebody else's platform — Aligned Aesthetics on `vagaro.com`,
Aesthetics Studio on `glossgenius.com`, Blendedbeauti on `skincaretherapy.net`, The Valley Spa Studio
on `gettimely.com`. Nothing published on a booking platform's domain can satisfy must-have 5, so
**these towns are structurally closed to an email channel rather than thin**, in the way the brief
describes Whistler as structurally closed. Two businesses in all three towns have sites of their own:
Excellence (silent across four pages) and Le Vestige (reachable, parked C). **I would mark Hanford,
Lemoore and Selma finished and not assign them again** — and note that a DM channel would open them
instantly, because a GlossGenius page always has an Instagram behind it.

**The privacy-policy-first rule produced ZERO addresses here, and that contradicts how the brief now
frames it.** The brief made the rule unconditional on 3 Nov on the strength of **six accepted addresses
off policies in Oklahoma, a market that published well** — and the explicit argument was that the rule
is not about scarcity. I ran it four times today: **The Spa at Fig Garden Village, Mystique, Savage
Serenity, and (as the no-policy fallback) Excellence's Terms of Use. Four fetches, no addresses.**
I am *not* proposing reverting to the conditional version — the 2 Nov conditional rule was built on two
data points and mine are four, so I would be repeating the same mistake in the opposite direction.
What I would add to the brief is the mechanism: a privacy policy names a contact for data requests,
and **a clinic that has decided its front door is the phone will satisfy that obligation with a phone
number**. All three policies I read did exactly that — Mystique's even says "contact us via the email
address or phone number given on our website" and then gives only a number. So the policy rule's yield
tracks **whether the market publishes mailboxes at all**, not whether the homepage happened to hide
one. Oklahoma publishes mailboxes; the Central Valley does not. The rule is still the right *next*
fetch — it costs one page and the alternative is nothing — but **budget it at Oklahoma's six-for-two
in the Midwest and South, and at my zero-for-four inland California.**

**A cheaper way to run the policy rule, which I would put in the brief.** Finding a policy link without
guessing a path normally costs a re-fetch of a page you have already read. Instead I spent **one
WebSearch with `allowed_domains` set to six parked clinic domains at once and the query "privacy policy
contact email address"**. It returned the exact policy URLs for two of them plus a contact page for a
third. One search, no guessed paths, no wasted fetches — and it scales to as many domains as you can
list. That is strictly better than the fetch-the-homepage-again route the brief implies.

**The deliberate directory fetch is a *local-association* technique, not a *chamber* one.** I spent
three directory fetches. The one that worked was **`oldtownclovis.org/salons-spas-yoga/`**, a
business-improvement-district listing, which gave **five clinic names in a town our files credited with
one** — and two of my seven rows (Maven Integrative, Brilyn) and both of my site-side errors came off
it. The two that produced **nothing new** were the **Visalia Chamber of Commerce** health listing (five
names, four already ours, one a dermatology group) and **`downtownvisalia.com/dtv_listings/`** (names
and addresses with no service descriptions, so unusable as a filter). The difference is that a chamber
lists whoever pays dues across every sector, while a district association lists the shops on its
street and groups them by what they do. **Look for the BID or main-street association, not the chamber.**

**Three same-name town catches in one sweep, and one of them is intra-state.** Clovis NM twice, Selma
TX once, plus Madera collapsing into Corte Madera. The area-code rule caught every one, and on both
New Mexico clinics it caught them before the address did — exactly as the brief promises. The new thing
is the **intra-state** pair: the brief's examples (Emerald NSW/QLD, Canyon Lake CA/TX, Clovis CA/NM) are
all cross-border, so the rule reads as a state-boundary problem. **Madera / Corte Madera is one state and
one area code region**, and only the town name in the address caught it. Worth adding, because a worker
reading the brief would have trusted the 559-vs-415 check that I happened not to need.

**Visalia's three-rows-from-140,000 result on 1 Nov was a one-off, and the town is now worked out.**
Query 4 returned five clinics and four were already in our files; the chamber and downtown directories
added nothing; of the two genuinely new Visalia businesses, one (LNM) publishes only a marketing
agency's mailbox in a meta tag and the other (DustyLynn) has no injectables. **Fresno's outer ring is
where the remaining supply is** — all three of my B rows are in Fresno or Clovis, from queries 5 and
10 — and **Madera is newly open**, with exactly one clinic found (Derm Maven MD, parked C on
dermatology) and no second query spent on it. **If anyone goes back, go to Madera and Fresno's north
side, not Visalia.**

**The neighbourhood-stacking technique did not transfer from Tulsa, and I think I know why.** The
3 Nov sweep reopened Tulsa by naming Brookside and Cherry Street. I tried the same on Fresno and Clovis
(Fig Garden, River Park, Woodward Park; Old Town, Sunnyside, Bullard). **Fig Garden / River Park /
Woodward Park worked** — it surfaced two new domains and got me into the north-Fresno cluster where my
best rows are. **Old Town / Sunnyside / Bullard failed outright**, collapsing into loyalty directories
and Clovis New Mexico. The ones that worked are **named shopping districts that businesses put in their
own addresses**; the ones that failed are residential areas and a street name. So the technique is
narrower than "name the neighbourhoods": **name the retail districts a clinic would print on its own
site.** And note that the modifier mattered more than the place names — "med spa rewards" dragged the
query into loyalty-programme land, while "medical spa injectables" kept it on clinics.

**"Rewards", "loyalty" and "membership" are now actively bad modifiers in the US.** The 2 Nov sweep
recommended "owner", "founder", "RN injector" and "rewards". Of those, **"owner" and "founder" were my
two best modifiers** (query 10, "Fresno Clovis independent medical spa injectables founded owner", was
the best query of the day with three new domains). **"Rewards" and "loyalty" both collapsed** — the
med-spa software industry (Boulevard, Pabau, ProspyrMed, Regulr, LoopyLoyalty, ScaleHaven) owns every
result for a scheme word plus a metro, and a loyalty-directory site returned the wrong state's Clovis.
**And "injector" plus "clinic" is worse still**: query 16 returned vascular surgery, nephrology and an
industrial medical clinic, because "clinic" in the Central Valley means a medical group. Recommend
the brief drop "rewards" from its modifier list and add a warning on "clinic".

**No page tried to steer the fetch and nothing looked compromised.** Nineteen businesses opened,
forty-three fetches, every one run with the data-not-instructions prompt in place. Two pages carried
**unreplaced vendor template text** — Cyrus Cosmetics prints "Placeholder for neck and jawline after
photograph. Replace before publishing", Excellence's Terms of Use names "Advice Media" as the
controller of the website, and Maven's About page carries a "Use to replace pic..." note in image text.
None of that is injected content; it is three sites mid-build, and it is flagged on the relevant rows.

**And the honest bottom line on volume.** I was asked for 15 to 25 rows and I have **seven, none of
them A**, from sixteen searches. I did not pad it. The constraint was not the fetch budget — I used 43
of 70 — it was that **after query 10 there was nothing left to look for**: five of my sixteen queries
returned not one in-market clinic, and four more returned only clinics already in our files. Taken with
1 Nov (fifteen accepted, eleven lost on the address) and 2 Nov (two rows from the California gaps), the
Central Valley has now had three passes and the supply curve has flattened. **I would call Visalia,
Hanford, Lemoore, Selma, Porterville, Tulare, Dinuba, Reedley, Kingsburg, Fowler and Selma finished,
and keep only Madera and north Fresno open** — and the thing worth more than another sourcing run here
is a decision on the phone and DM channel, because this market's best clinics (Excellence in Hanford,
Mystique and Savage Serenity in Fresno, Kiss Me behind Cloudflare) are all reachable by a human and
none of them by email.
