## What the market taught me

**1. Long Island is as rich as the brief hoped, and the grep was right that it was untouched.**
"Long Island", "Nassau", "Garden City", "Manhasset", "Great Neck", "Massapequa", "Smithtown",
"Syosset", "Bellmore" and "Merrick" all returned zero prior hits. 13 searches and 42 fetches
produced **17 accepted rows** — the best rows-per-fetch of any US market in the file that I can
see — and I stopped on judgement, not budget (see point 10).

**2. THE WORST SAME-NAME TRAP IN THE MARKET IS "ROCKVILLE CENTRE" → "ROCKVILLE, MARYLAND", and
it cost a whole query.** A stacked query naming Smithtown, Commack, Port Washington and Rockville
Centre returned **seven of ten results in Rockville, MD** — ReNew You, Aesthetic & Dermatology
Center, Faulkner Plastic Surgery, The Beauty Bay, The Medical Skin Clinic — including
`bellablissmedspa.com`, which is **already pipeline row 211 as a Rockville MD clinic**. The area
code does not save you (both are outside any shared region) but the town name alone destroys the
query. **Say "Rockville Centre NY", or better, pair it only with other Nassau towns.** Add
Rockville Centre to the same-name list beside Clovis NM, Corte Madera and Victoria.

**3. A NEW, EIGHTH FETCH-FAILURE MODE: CleanTalk email encoding.** The Skin Clinic Huntington
renders its policy mailbox as `th*****************@gm***.com` and says so outright — *"This
contact has been encoded by CleanTalk"* — with a **different** masked address behind the
`mailto:`. It is not Cloudflare, not client-side rendering, not silence, not a site error, not an
interstitial, and not mode seven. It behaves exactly like Cloudflare: not seen, never recorded,
**browser-recoverable**, so browser-visit list. **Recommend adding CleanTalk beside Cloudflare in
the taxonomy**, and note the wrinkle that the two masked addresses sit on different domains, so a
human recovering it must still apply the "whose domain is it" test.

**4. THE PRIVACY-POLICY ADDRESS RULE IS A HIGH-YIELD RULE ON LONG ISLAND: 4 hits from 9 policies,
about 44%** — better than Arizona's one in three and far better than inland California's zero.
It produced **Bella NYC** (the only mailbox on that whole site), **Nova Med Spa**
(`admin@`, nominated as the data-request route), **Garden City Medical Spa** (nominated outright),
and **Applied Aesthetic** (a hit that Cloudflare voided). The five misses all satisfied the
data-request duty exactly as the stated mechanism predicts — a phone number (VITRA, Youthology
via a form), a postal address plus phone (Beauty Bomb), a bare "contact Us" (Angelic), or a
missing string (Nimbus). **Budget this rule HIGH in Nassau and Suffolk.**

**5. The free CRM-detection pass is worth more here than the address sometimes is.** Three
policies named their stack outright: Nova Med Spa names **Twilio** for SMS and email delivery,
which tells us a programmatic two-way SMS channel is already provisioned at that clinic — exactly
what the offer needs. Garden City Medical Spa names **Termly**, Google Maps Platform and Google
Analytics. Bella NYC names **Boulevard** as its payment and booking provider in the policy text,
which is far stronger evidence than a `blvd.me` URL inference. Read the processor list every time.

**6. MUST-HAVE 4 IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT ON LONG ISLAND, NOT MUST-HAVE 2 OR 5 — and this is
the mirror image of the British diagnosis.** Seven of 17 accepted rows are C, and **six of those
seven are C on must-have 4 alone** (the seventh, Legacy, fails must-have 2 and 4 together).
Only **two businesses in the entire market published a founding year** (The Skin Clinic's 2009,
in a staff bio — and it is a near-miss; The Sonu Spa's 2023 copyright — also a near-miss), and
only **six published a review count**. Long Island clinics publish their owners, their platforms
and their membership schemes freely and almost never publish their age. **That is a publishing
habit, not a business fact**, and it collides head-on with the evidence ladder. Do not read a
C-heavy Long Island run as a weak market, and do not pad a row to B to fix it.

**7. The banked-credit signal is alive and well in Nassau, and it has a name here.** TWO separate
clinics run a scheme called **"The Beauty Bank"** — Applied Aesthetic in Garden City and The
Natural Beauty Med Spa in Huntington — neither affiliated with the other. That is the brief's
"wallet / bank / vault" affluent-suburb technique confirming itself in a new market, from the
other direction: I never ran the wallet query, and the schemes turned up anyway because the
postcodes support them. Worth running the wallet query here on a second pass.

**8. NO DOMINANT PLATFORM, which confirms the per-market finding again.** Across 24 businesses:
GlossGenius ×3, Boulevard ×4 (three of them `blvd.me` URL inferences, one named in text),
Aesthetic Record ×4, Meevo ×2, and one each of Zenoti, Mangomint, MyAestheticsPro, MyPatientNow,
RepeatMD, Vagaro, Podium, Symplast, Elyon and Tebra — plus **four clinics with no identifiable
platform at all** (Rethink, Spa Cosmedic, SM Aesthetics, Lavender Lush), every one of them with
inert Book Now buttons. **Two candidates for the grade-A nameable-system list, each seen with a
real tenant ID: Meevo (Millennium)**, which at Garden City Medical Spa and VITA serves the diary,
the gift cards AND the memberships from one tenant — which is exactly "a patient list in a
queryable place" — and **Symplast**, a full aesthetics practice-management and EMR platform, at
Boost Your Beauty. **Elyon** (`elyonhq.com`) is a platform I have not seen before and could not
identify from the page; worth someone looking at it.

**9. The gmail/yahoo rate is this market's signature and it belongs on every row.** Eight of the
17 accepted mailboxes are consumer gmail or yahoo addresses published on the clinic's own domain
— Aesthetic Arts, Rethink, Natural Beauty, Spa Cosmedic (yahoo), SM Aesthetics, Garden City
Medical Spa, Legacy, and the ruled-out Great Neck Medical Spa. All pass must-have 5 on both of
its real tests (published on their own page; mail reaches them), and none is a generic industry
domain or an agency mailbox, so the `medspas.info` ruling does not bite. But every one of them
means a reply lands in a personal inbox rather than a monitored shared one, which affects how the
first email should be written. It is recorded on each row.

**10. WHERE I STOPPED AND WHY.** The first 20 fetches produced 10 accepted rows. The next 16
produced 5. The last 6 produced 2 — Lavender Lush and nothing else — and three of those six
(Angelic's contact form, Rejuv's policy, Beauty Lab's contact page) confirmed failures rather
than buying rows. **That is the marginal fetch stopping paying, so I stopped**, four searches and
eight fetches inside the budget rather than spending them.

**WHAT I WOULD DO NEXT, in cost order.** (1) **One fetch: `thesonuspa.com/locations`** — a named
MD, a three-year copyright, an immaculate menu and a free-consultation offer, blocked only by a
missing contact URL. The cheapest outstanding lead in the market. (2) **One fetch:
`medspaofnewyork.com/privacy/`** — settles both its market and its address. (3) **Hand Jess the
browser-visit list in this order: Applied Aesthetic (Cloudflare, and it is the best row Long
Island has), The Skin Clinic Huntington (CleanTalk), Rejuv Aesthetix (client-side).** Three
browser minutes could add a grade A and two Bs. (4) **Untouched towns**, every one of which still
greps to zero: Oceanside, Long Beach, Lynbrook's neighbours Hewlett and Woodmere, Hicksville,
Levittown, Wantagh, East Setauket, Stony Brook, Sayville, Riverhead, and Southampton and
Westhampton proper — the Hamptons query I did run returned a dead domain, two listicles and a
massage practice, so the Hamptons are **thin rather than unworked**. (5) **Try the
neighbourhood/main-street technique properly here, because I only sampled it.** Every accepted
row on this run sits on a named main street — Plandome Road, Middle Neck Road, Merrick Road,
Jericho Turnpike, Franklin Avenue, East Main Street, Nassau Boulevard. Long Island clinics
self-describe by their village main street, which is exactly the "names locals trade under"
condition the Tulsa Brookside result turned on. Query **"Plandome Road", "Americana Manhasset",
"Seventh Street Garden City", "Main Street Bay Shore"** rather than the town names again.

### Noise, and what to block

Add to `blocked_domains`: `medspascout.com`, `thecliniccompass.com`, `bestofnj.com`
("New Jersey's Best Medical Spas of 2026" — the sponsored-listicle hazard), `bestofessex.com`,
`monmouthhealthandwellness.com`, `businessyab.com`, `threebestrated.com`, `medspa.com`,
`princetonequity.com` and `princetonmedspapartners.com` (the PE roll-up already in the file as a
Huntsville near-miss — **its name alone takes a Princeton slot**), `alle.com` (its provider-locator
town pages), `themontclairgirl.com` and `themonmouthmoms.com` (local blog "where to get" and
"salon + spa guide" listicles — the coin-flip hazard), and `montclaircenter.com/directory-bid`
(a business-improvement-district directory whose only med spa listing was a chain, so the
district-association technique that worked in Clovis **did not** work here).

**AND A NEW NOISE CLASS: COSMETIC DENTISTRY.** The combination of "aesthetics" with an affluent New
Jersey town name pulls **dentists** hard — `eislerdental.com` took two of ten slots on the Tenafly
query, and `academydentalcare.com`, `englewoodcliffsdentistry.com`, `morriseyeassociates.com`
("Ocular Aesthetics"), `familyofcaring.com` and `inspirewellness.com` (counselling) took one each
across three queries. In an affluent suburb every trade markets itself as "aesthetics". Block the
dental domains as you meet them, or add "injector" rather than "aesthetics" as the modifier.

---

## What this market taught me

**The affluent ring is not where the rows are — they are one town out, and that is a structural
fact rather than bad luck.** Of 15 accepted rows, the twelve assigned core towns produced only
**six**: Montclair 1, Englewood 2, Morristown 1, Madison/Livingston 1, Westfield 1. The other nine
came from **one ring further out** — Verona/West Caldwell, Randolph ×2, Mountainside, Woodcliff
Lake, Red Bank, Princeton Junction, Highland Park and Hamilton. **And the correction to the 26 Oct
read matters.** That sweep said "Montclair, Summit, Short Hills and Red Bank deserve their own query
each". I gave Montclair and Red Bank their own query and each produced exactly one sendable row.
**Short Hills and Summit produced ZERO own-town rows across three queries between them** — every
Short Hills result was either an **SEO suburb page belonging to a clinic in Millburn, Mountainside or
Morristown**, or a national chain's location page; and the one clinic actually at a Summit address
was a nail-and-waxing day spa. **SHORT HILLS AND SUMMIT ARE SEO-FARMED, NOT THIN.** The affluent town
name is a keyword that clinics in cheaper towns rank for, which is the **mirror image** of the Tulsa
neighbourhood finding: there, local names surfaced clinics a city name had hidden; here, the
prestige name surfaces clinics that are not in it. **Do not query those two towns again. Query the
towns around them** — Mountainside, Westfield, Verona, West Caldwell, Randolph and Denville all
produced.

**Tenafly, Westwood and Chatham are SILENT rather than unworked, in the Kirkland sense.** Every
clinic I found in them publishes no email: Ledo (Westwood), The Skin Lounge (Chatham), Le Ami
(Tenafly, not trading at all). Those are browser or phone jobs, not sourcing jobs.

**THE PRIVACY-POLICY ADDRESS RULE YIELDED ZERO FROM FOUR POLICIES, AND THE MECHANISM HELD EXACTLY AS
THE BRIEF PREDICTS RATHER THAN FAILING MYSTERIOUSLY.** Naturally Aesthetic's policy routes data
requests to `/contact`; Eminence's routes them to a **postal** address; Salt & Sky's is WordPress
boilerplate nominating **no route at all**; and Ledo's "policy" is the hibu platform's generic page,
not the clinic's at all. **So New Jersey behaves like inland California and Utah, not like Oklahoma
— budget this fetch at near zero here.** But the useful half: the Salt & Sky case is **the first
time I have seen a no-route policy actually license the 8 Nov widened `/contact` exception**, and I
spent that `/contact` fetch legitimately — and it was still a form. The exception is correctly
worded; it just does not pay in this market.

**The US `/contact` rule held for a sixth consecutive sweep.** Fourteen of 15 accepted rows had the
address off a homepage, an About page, a membership page or an SEO suburb page footer. The one
`/contact` fetch made as a **first** move — Summit Aesthetics MD, whose homepage never surfaced in
search — produced an address, exactly as the 2 Nov exception predicts. The two made as retries
produced one address (FACE Aesthetic Artistry, whose contact page was the only URL that surfaced at
all) and one nothing (Salt & Sky).

**A NEW AND CHEAP ADDRESS SOURCE: AN SEO SUBURB PAGE CARRIES THE FULL SITE FOOTER.** Two accepted
rows (Zen Aesthetics, Fortress Medical Aesthetics) and one rule-out (House of Ness) gave up their
mailbox, their full menu, their founder bio, their platform and their site count on an "areas
served" page, because those pages are generated from the site template rather than hand-written.
The brief currently treats `areas-served/<town>` page sets purely as crowders-out to block in query
one. **They are that, and once one has surfaced it is as good an address fetch as the homepage and
sometimes better**, because it also prints the clinic's own list of claimed towns, which is what you
need in order to count sites. The exception is a page set on a site that is not built yet — see Le
Ami above.

**THE VOS-STYLE PARENT-GROUP LOYALTY FOOTER DID NOT FIRE ONCE in 15 accepted rows, and I looked on
every single one.** What fired instead, twice, was a **manufacturer's** programme being present and
correctly not counting (Allē at House of Ness, Evolus Rewards at Atrium). And what fired twice as a
genuine group tell was **something the brief does not yet name: a cross-brand sister business linked
from the footer's "Main Page" or "Shop" slot.** Medi Spa by SDP's footer "Main Page" link goes to
`salondipanache.com`, the salon that owns it; MedSpa by Beauty Bar's birthday gift card is
redeemable at its sister salon group. **Suggested addition to the brief: in the US, read the
footer's "Main Page", "Shop" and "Our Family of Brands" links, not only the loyalty slot — a salon
parent hides there, where a med spa roll-up hides in the loyalty link.**

**MUST-HAVE 4 WAS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IN THIS MARKET, as in Britain but for a different reason.**
Five of my six parked C rows fail on must-have 4 and only one on must-have 2. Only **four** of 15
accepted rows published a founding year or equivalent (Elizabeth Roche 2007; Montclair Rejuvenation
February 2017, **found on a sibling clinic's site**; Zen Aesthetics 2021; Englewood "10+ Years /
4,000+ Patients"), and only **three** published a review count (The Aesthetic Bar 250+, Elizabeth
Roche 113, Princeton Aesthetics 81+). Britain's problem is that busy clinics do not print the
number; **New Jersey's problem is that the number is printed and BROKEN**. Three sites' own
statistics counters render as **"0 +"** or **"0 Total Reviews"** while the page displays real
testimonials — The Aesthetic Bar (years, units and clients all zero), Serenity, and Atrium's
"Brand new" reviewer note pulling against its 110 reviews. **A broken counter is not a low count
and must not be read as one**; it is the same class of artifact as a stale copyright and should be
recorded as "counter broken", not as "no reviews".

**No platform concentration, confirming the 8 Nov per-market correction.** Across 15 rows:
Boulevard 3, Jane 2, Meevo 2, GlossGenius 1, MyAestheticsPro 1, AdvancedMD 1, Zenoti 1 plus 1
probable — and **five rows with no identifiable platform at all**. That last number is the one to
carry into a pitch: **a third of New Jersey's independents book on their own domain with nothing
nameable behind it**, so the offer cannot assume a queryable list exists. Moxie turned up once more
(on a near-miss), which is now its third or later sighting since being added on 8 Nov.

**The gmail mailbox is common here and is a finding, not a defect.** Three of 15 rows publish only a
consumer mailbox whose local part is the clinic's own name — `imagerevolutionhealth@gmail.com`,
`fortressmedicalaesthetics@gmail.com`, and `staff4gor@gmail.com` on a rule-out. All are recordable
under the ICP (published visibly, on the clinic's own page, not a generic industry domain and not an
agency's), all are one step weaker than an own-domain mailbox, and none may be "corrected". A fourth
row publishes an own-brand but **different** domain (`info@mrcenter.co` against a site at
`montclairrejuvenationcenter.com`), which is the ordinary mismatch the ICP says to record as printed.

**Fetch-failure picture:** no client-side rendering, no interstitials, no site-side errors. **Two
Cloudflare cases** (Menon Medispa, House of Ness) and **one `robots_disallowed`** (Princeton Medi
Spa). **In both Cloudflare cases the helper did NOT volunteer a decode** — it stated outright that
the address was hidden and that it had not decoded it, I did not ask it to, and no address was
recorded from either. New Jersey's dominant failure mode is the usual American one: plain silence,
a form and a phone number.

**One same-name catch, and the pattern is worth more than the clinic.** "Summit Aesthetics MD"
trades in **Hamilton, Mercer County**, about forty miles from Summit; the 609 area code was the tell
before the postal address was. **AFFLUENT NEW JERSEY TOWN NAMES ARE USED AS BRAND NAMES BY CLINICS
ELSEWHERE IN THE STATE** — Summit, Princeton and Montclair all appeared in the names of clinics not
in those towns (Montclair Rejuvenation Center is in Verona and West Caldwell; Princeton Medi Spa and
Princeton Aesthetics are in Princeton and Princeton Junction respectively; Bergen County Medical Spa
is in Fair Lawn). **Read the postal address, never the brand**, and in this state the area code
settles the county before the address does.

**Where the depth is, for whoever goes next.** **Denville and Randolph are the richest unworked
pocket** — Randolph alone gave two accepted rows and Denville gave two clinics that need one policy
fetch each (Joven, Exhibit), which are the two cheapest outstanding leads in the state. **The
bank/wallet/vault query should be run FIRST in any affluent US suburb ring**: one search produced
seven clinic domains including two accepted rows and the richest dormant structure in the run — but
it is a **national** query, so budget a placing step, because one of its seven was Colorado and
three could not be placed at all. **Monmouth County is barely touched**: one query produced one A
row and three rule-outs, and Rumson, Fair Haven, Little Silver, Holmdel and Middletown were never
queried on their own. **Princeton has more left** behind a robots refusal and a silent clinic with
thirteen published years. And **Hoboken, Jersey City and the Gold Coast were deliberately left
alone** — they are the 26 Oct sweep's ground and already carry five pipeline rows.

---

# Recovery run near-misses — 9 November 2026

Standard applied: ICP v2 with every ruling in `outputs/pipeline/ICP.md` as of 9 Nov 2026, including
the seventh address look-alike (`sms:` href), the market-type correction to must-have 4 evidence,
the "dermatology is a hiring credential in a wealthy market" validation, Meevo and Symplast on the
platform list, and NYSHIP as a must-have 2 detector. Fetch rules and the eight fetch-failure modes
from `reference/clinic-sourcing-brief.md`.

Every entry below names its failing must-have by number. Nothing here carries a question for a
person: each is a decision, with the single check that would reverse it where one exists.

## A. Group A recovery candidates that do not qualify

### Skinly Aesthetics — Upper East Side, New York, NY · `skinlyaesthetics.com`
**FAILS MUST-HAVE 4.** No dated or quantified artifact of any kind on the clinic's own site.

- 157 East 64th Street, 2nd floor, New York, NY 10065. One address; `/location/upper-east-side/`
  is that one site, not a second.
- **Must-have 5 PASSES and the September note was right about this one:**
  `info@skinlyaesthetics.com` was read verbatim as visible text and as a `mailto:` on
  `https://skinlyaesthetics.com/`, 9 Nov 2026. Nothing obfuscated, no mask, no meta-tag-only case.
  The address is kept here so the call is reversible.
- Must-have 1 passes: Botox, Dysport and the full filler range head the menu.
- Must-have 2 passes, caveat recorded: the only named therapeutic indications are **hyperhidrosis**
  and **TMJ** (plus Upneeq, arguably a third). That is two to three incidental lines, inside the
  four-indication threshold, which passes as written. No insurance, Medicare or named scheme
  anywhere; financing is Cherry and CareCredit, i.e. cash-pay consumer credit. Semaglutide,
  tirzepatide, BHRT and NAD+ are cash-pay wellness lines with no reimbursement language.
- **The "Cosmetic Dermatology" label was tested and cleared**, which is the sixth market this
  shape has been caught in: the clinic calls itself a "Cosmetic Dermatology Clinic" and the page
  never calls Dr Schwarzburg a dermatologist, lists nothing surgical ("non-surgical" repeatedly),
  names no mole, lesion or skin-cancer service and bills no insurance. Label, not finding.
- **Why it fails:** no founding year, no "since", no "established", no "over N years", **no review
  count**, no star rating, no dated client reviews, no award years, and **no footer copyright year
  at all**. Press logos (Good Housekeeping, Harper's Bazaar, Forbes) are undated. Dr Schwarzburg is
  "Ivy League-educated and board-certified" with no career length given, so even the ladder's
  middle rung is unavailable.
- **The single check that would release it:** a founding year or a review count on an About or team
  page. **One search was spent looking for one and bought nothing** — a site-limited search of
  `skinlyaesthetics.com` for "about us founded year reviews our team" returned ten treatment pages
  and no About or team page at all. That negative result is itself worth recording: this is a
  clinic with 40-odd service pages and no page about itself.
- Textbook instance of the 9 Nov market-type finding: Upper East Side Manhattan, an affluent
  referral-driven market, and must-have 4 on evidence is the only thing that failed it.
- Dormant signal is real and would have made a good row: "Join the Exclusive Skinly Club", a $50
  first-visit credit for subscribers, 0% financing.

### Manhattan Medspa — New York, NY · `manhattan-medspa.com`
**FAILS MUST-HAVE 5**, and also fails must-have 4.

- 220 Madison Ave. Suite C, New York, NY 10016. One address.
- **Must-have 5: no email address anywhere on the homepage, in any form** — not visible text, not a
  `mailto:`, not an `sms:` href, not a meta tag, and not masked or Cloudflare-protected. Simply
  absent. The only contact routes are "Request an Appointment" and two phone numbers (new patients
  and existing patients).
- Must-have 4 also fails: "with years of outstanding service behind us" and no number, no founding
  year, no review count, no star rating, no dated reviews, a Marie Claire badge with no year, and a

- Must-have 1 passes (wrinkle relaxers and dermal fillers head the menu). Must-have 3 passes (one
  site). Must-have 2 passes: Sclerotherapy sits under a "Vein Therapy" heading, and **prominence is

  appear nowhere on the site, and neither does insurance, so the 8 Nov closing rule resolves it in
  the clinic's favour.
- **No privacy-policy fetch was spent**, deliberately. The unconditional rule says a silent
  homepage earns a policy fetch, but must-have 4 fails independently here, so the row would be C
  with or without an address. Recorded as a judgement, not an omission.
- **This is the second of the three "grade-C fallbacks with real published emails" to turn out not
  to have one.** See the note at the end of this file.

### Dr Tass Cosmetic & Skin Clinics — Southbank / Port Melbourne / Ripponlea, VIC · `drtass.com.au`
**FAILS MUST-HAVE 1 — a surgical arm, on substance rather than on a word.**

- The 24 Sep drop reason was correctly identified as a non-must-have ("bookings are taken by
  phone"). That reason is dead. The clinic still fails, for a different and better reason.
- Three Melbourne clinics, so **must-have 3 passes on count**: Crown Spa (Crown Towers L3, 8
  Whiteman Street, Southbank 3006), 101 Beach Street Port Melbourne 3207, 100 Brighton Road
  Ripponlea 3185, all on one phone number.
- **Must-have 5 PASSES and the address is kept here so the call is reversible:**
  `enquiries@drtass.com.au` was read verbatim as visible footer text and as a `mailto:` on
  `https://drtass.com.au/contact/`, 9 Nov 2026. A second visible address, `marketing@drtass.com.au`,
  is published on the same page for PR enquiries.
- **Must-have 6 would also have passed:** the contact page carries no statement refusing
  unsolicited commercial email or marketing, and the address is on the clinic's own site, not a
  directory. Recorded because it was checked, not because it matters now.
- Must-have 2 was screened and is not the failure: no Medicare, bulk billing, health-fund or
  insurance language anywhere; "Spider Veins & Capillaries" with no varicose or venous-disease
  language passes under the 5 Nov vein rule; "Excessive Sweating (Hyperhidrosis)" is one named
  indication, inside the four-indication threshold.
- **Why it fails must-have 1.** The navigation carries a top-level **"Surgical"** item, and a
  site-limited search of `drtass.com.au` resolved it from the result titles alone, for zero
  fetches: `drtass.com.au/dr-tass-cosmetic-clinics-surgical/` exists, alongside
  `/treatments/hair-transplant-treatment/`, `/treatments/hair-transplant/` and a published
  "How Much Does a Hair Transplant Cost in Australia?" guide. **Hair transplantation is excision
  with closure**, and the 8 Nov ruling is explicit that excision is surgery regardless of what the
  heading calls it — the converse of the Peterborough case, where cosmetic blemish work passes
  despite using the words "minor surgery". This is not one line bolted onto an injectables clinic:
  it is a dedicated surgical section of the business with its own marketing funnel. A second
  doctor, Dr Vikram Jayaprakash, has his own About page.
- The decision was close and is recorded as a decision. The counter-argument is real — Dr Tass
  bills no insurance and carries no disease caseload, which are the two reasons the ICP gives for
  the surgery and dermatology disqualifications — and if the standard is ever narrowed to a pure
  billing test, this row comes back with everything else already verified.
  **DISQUALIFIED UNDER ICP v2 - FAILS MUST-HAVE 1**
- Dormant signal, recorded in case the call is revisited: "DR TASS SIGNATURE CLUB", a named
  subscriber scheme.

## B. Group C — the two fetch-failure retries

### The Skin Care Clinic — Hobart, TAS · `theskincareclinic.com.au`
**FAILS MUST-HAVE 1. The brief's premise for this clinic is wrong: it was never blocked only by a
fetch failure.**

- The homepage fetched cleanly on 9 Nov 2026, so there is no fetch failure to classify and this is
  **not** a browser-visit candidate. The blocker is qualification, not tooling.
- **Injectables are not mentioned anywhere on the site.** The menu is "In Clinic Skin Treatments",
  "Skin Consultations", "Facial Treatments", "Acne Treatments" and "Cosmetic Therapies". Staff are
  a "Dermal Therapist" and "trained skin technicians". **No doctor, no nurse, no prescriber is
  named anywhere** — the only personal name on the page is "Meg", in a customer testimonial.
- That fails must-have 1 on its own terms rather than on a label: must-have 1 exists because
  injectables wear off on a three-to-four month cycle, which is what makes a lapsed list worth
  recalling. A dermal-therapy and retail-skincare clinic has no such cycle. Afterpay and ZIP Pay
  are the only payment lines; product sales (Osmosis, ZO) are a large part of the business.
- Must-have 5 also fails: **no email address anywhere on the homepage** in any form, and **no
  street address either**. September's `/contact/` page was never the only gap.
- Must-have 4 is unresolved and moot: a meta description claiming "20 years in skin care", no
  founding year, no review count, no dated reviews, a bare "© 2026".
- Must-have 6 recorded because it was checked: no statement refusing unsolicited commercial email
  appears on the homepage.
- September called it "the best dormant signal in Tasmania" and the loyalty scheme is real —
  "Loyalty Rewards" / "My Loyalty Rewards" points plus a "Gift E-Certificate". A good dormant
  signal on a clinic in the wrong business is still the wrong business.
  **DISQUALIFIED UNDER ICP v2 - FAILS MUST-HAVE 1**

### Illuminate Skin Clinic — Kings Hill, Kent · `illuminateskinclinic.co.uk`
**FAILS MUST-HAVE 5 on a fetch failure. GOES ON THE BROWSER-VISIT LIST — see section D.**
Not a near-miss on the merits; the merits are excellent.

- **The domain was found, and it is not what two earlier runs guessed.** It is
  `illuminateskinclinic.co.uk` — **"clinic", singular**. A batched `allowed_domains` search on the
  plural `illuminateskinclinics.co.uk` returned nothing, which is probably why 23 Sep and 9 Nov
  both ran out of budget on it. One ordinary search found it immediately. Recorded so nobody
  spends a third run on the guess.
- Must-have 4 passes outright and strongly: **"Founded by Dr Sophie Shotter in 2014"** plus award
  years 2015, 2016, 2017 and 2019 including "Aesthetic Award For Best Clinic South 2019". Twelve
  years of trading, on the clinic's own page, on the ladder's top rung.
- Must-have 1 passes. Must-have 3 passes: one site, Kings Hill, Kent; Dr Sophie Shotter is
  "Medical Director and Founder of Illuminate", one decision-maker.
- Must-have 2 passes: no insurance, no NHS, and no vein, mole, lesion, skin-cancer or surgical line
  anywhere on the homepage.
- **Must-have 5 fails on tooling.** No email address on the homepage in any form. `/contact`
  returns **401** to a fetch (the 23 Sep finding, reproduced). `/privacy-policy` — the exact URL a
  search returned, not a guessed path — returns **client_error**. So the homepage serves while two
  subpages refuse an automated agent.
- **Which failure mode:** an access refusal, the same family as the sixth mode (challenge
  interstitial) rather than the seventh. **It is NOT mode seven**: no policy was ever read, so no
  policy nominated an email route and then omitted the address. A 401 is addressed to our fetcher
  and a person's browser clears it, so this is browser-recoverable and does not belong in
  near-misses on the merits.
- Must-have 8 is unresolved: no "Ltd", "Limited", company number or registered name on the
  homepage, and the policy that would normally carry it could not be read. A UK row cannot be
  graded without it, so Jess's browser visit should read the footer and the policy together.

### Med Spa of New York · `medspaofnewyork.com`
**UNRESOLVED on must-have 5. The named fetch failed.** No disposition change.

## D. Belongs on the browser-visit list

These four are **not** near-misses on the merits. Each fails must-have 5 only because the page did
not ship the characters, and each is recoverable by a person opening it. Added to
`outputs/pipeline/browser-visit-list.md` is the caller's edit to make; the evidence is here.

### 1. No.6 Clinic — Tunbridge Wells, Kent · `no6clinic.co.uk` — **the best of the four**
Group E resolved: **must-have 1 PASSES on substance and the September label was wrong.**

- The September rule-out read "beauty-led rather than medical", a bare label with no evidence
  behind it. Read today, the treatment menu says the opposite. **Injectables are the first and
  largest category**: "Anti-Wrinkle Injections", "Dermal Fillers", "8 Point Face Lift", "Profhilo",
  "Polynucleotides (Plinest)", "Sculptra", "Sunekos", "Excessive Sweating". There is **no waxing,
  no lashes, no nails, no massage and no tanning on the site at all**. Staff are "medical director
  Dr Natasha Gilani" and a "Nurse manager Samantha".
- **The label here was the clinic's own trading name** — the site brands itself "NO.6 BEAUTY
  CLINIC" and is a medical aesthetics clinic. That is the strongest instance of "a label is not a
  finding" measured so far, because the misleading word was not in a meta description or a heading
  but in the business's name. Worth adding to the ruling's examples.
- Must-have 4 passes outright: **"has been an established medical aesthetic clinic for 20 years"**,
  a years-in-business claim about the business, the ladder's top rung. Dated reviews exist
  (11/02/2026, 9/04/2026, 8/14/2026) but are all 2026 and add nothing.
- Must-have 2 passes, and two separate rules did the work: "Red Thread Vein Removal",
  "Thermavein" and "Vascular IPL" are **named in the brief as cash-pay everywhere we sell**, and
  "Excessive Sweating" is one named indication, inside the four-indication threshold. No insurance,
  no NHS anywhere on the page.
- Must-have 3 passes: one address, Clayfield Mews, Newcomen Road, Tunbridge Wells TN4 9PA; one
  decision-maker.
- **Must-have 5 fails: the address is Cloudflare-obfuscated.** The header and footer both render
  `[email protected]`, linked to a `/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#` path. **The page did not ship
  the characters, so the address is NOT SEEN** — and nothing is recorded here. **Our fetch helper
  did not offer a decode and none was taken.**

## E. The brief's own claim about Group A, which was not true

**The near-misses file never recorded an address or a URL for any of the three American Group A
clinics**, although it twice asserts otherwise.

The 24 Sep section heads them "Three grade-C fallbacks with **real published emails**", the 9 Nov
re-read says "All three **already have published addresses recorded**", and the section-4 summary
repeats "They have addresses recorded already." Grepped and read in place on 9 Nov 2026: the file
contains, for Aesthé By MD, Manhattan Medspa and Skinly Aesthetics, **no email address, no domain
and no URL** — only the clinic names, a site count or a membership note, and the assertion.

Measured outcome of the three one-fetch recoveries that assertion promised:

| Clinic | Address actually published? | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Aesthé By MD / Osphere Med Aesthetics | **Yes** — two, one per brand | Sendable B (new row) |
| Skinly Aesthetics | **Yes** — visible text and `mailto:` | C on **must-have 4** |
| Manhattan Medspa | **No** — none on the homepage in any form | C on **must-have 5** |

So the claim was two-thirds true as a statement about the clinics and **entirely untrue as a
statement about the file** — and the difference matters, because the promised cost was one fetch
each and the real cost was a search to find each domain plus one to three fetches. Both Australian
Group A entries behaved the same way: names and suburbs recorded, no domain, no address.

**The general form, which is the part worth keeping:** a near-miss entry that says a clinic has a
published address without printing the address is not a recoverable lead, it is a lead that has to
be re-found. The fix is mechanical — **print the address and the URL in the entry, or do not claim
one exists.** Every entry in this file prints what it found.

## 10 November 2026 — the six AU/NZ single operators ICP v2 left behind

# AU/NZ recovery run — near misses

**Run date: 2026-11-10.** Search-weighted recovery of the six Australian and New Zealand
clinics dropped in September 2026 under the "single operators" rule that ICP v2 abolished on
16 Oct 2026. Five of the six did not qualify; one (Sapphire Appearance Medicine, Auckland) is
in `aunz-recovery.json` as a grade B.

**Premise check first, because the brief asked for it.** All six were genuinely dropped on the
single-operator rule and nothing else — I read every entry. Two corrections to the commission,
both detailed at the end of this file: one of the six had already been partially opened, and
"never opened at all" is therefore not true of it; and a seventh name sits beside them in the
same bullets which is disqualified rather than recoverable, which the file already flags.

**Where C rows live.** Every clinic below is in this file, including the ones that fail exactly
one must-have and are therefore **C, parked, not dropped**. `aunz-recovery.json` holds only the
sendable row. Each entry below prints the address, the URL and the consent findings in full, so a
C can be promoted later without re-researching it.

**No email address anywhere in this file was constructed, guessed or inferred**, and no decode of
any masked or obfuscated address was offered to me or taken. Nothing in this run was
Cloudflare-obfuscated or CleanTalk-masked: where an address is absent below, the page genuinely
published none, which is a different problem and **not** a browser-visit problem.

## 1. DC Aesthetics — Ashmore, Gold Coast, QLD · `dcaesthetics.com.au`

**Grade C. Failing must-have: must-have 4.** Exactly one must-have fails, so this is parked and
recoverable, not dropped.

- **Domain resolved:** `dcaesthetics.com.au` (no domain had ever been recorded for this clinic).
  Footer brand name: "DC Aesthetics Injectables & Skin Gold Coast". The "DC" is the owner's
  initials — **Diana Cern**.
- **Published address, printed in full as required:** **12 Warrungen Way, Ashmore, Gold Coast,
  Queensland 4214**, read off <https://dcaesthetics.com.au/contact/> on 2026-11-10. Postcode 4214
  and the suburb name confirm the Gold Coast, Queensland. Phone 0421 774 279.
- **Email: PUBLISHED AND SEEN.** `info@dcaesthetics.com.au`, printed as plain text on the clinic's
  own contact page at <https://dcaesthetics.com.au/contact/>, read 2026-11-10. The page shipped the
  real characters — not a `[email protected]` render, not a Cloudflare email-protection token, not
  a CleanTalk mask. **Email can reach this clinic.** It is not masked and it is not absent.
- **AU/NZ must-have 6, finding (a) — address provenance:** the address above was read off the
  clinic's **own** site, its contact page, and is repeated on its homepage. Not a directory, not a
  social profile, not a meta tag, not a QR code.
- **AU/NZ must-have 6, finding (b) — consent screen:** **no** "no unsolicited commercial email"
  notice and no anti-spam or refusal-to-receive wording of any kind on either the contact page or
  the homepage. There is **no privacy policy on the site at all** — none is linked from either page
  — so the policy route was unavailable rather than skipped. Nothing on either page is a refusal to
  receive; there is no marketing-promise wording to quote in either direction. Both must-have 6
  findings are clear.
- **Must-haves that pass:** must-have 1 (injectables-led: wrinkle treatments, bio-remodelling,
  biostimulators, PDO threads, PRP/PRF, peels — no beauty-salon menu, no surgery, no disease
  language); must-have 2 (no Medicare, no HICAPS, no health fund, no bulk billing anywhere in the
  text, and no therapeutic indication named at all — no migraine, hyperhidrosis, TMJ, veins or mole
  checks); must-have 3 (**one** site. The suburb links — Broadbeach Waters, Helensvale, Labrador,
  Nerang, Robina — are SEO service-area pages off one address, which is the first of the three
  look-alikes must-have 3 names, and one owner-injector still decides marketing); must-have 5 (above).
- **WHY IT FAILS MUST-HAVE 4, and I am not softening it.** The clinic publishes **no dated or
  quantified artifact of any kind** on either page I read: no founding year, no "established" or
  "since" claim, **no copyright year or range at all** (the footer says only "proudly powered by
  WordPress"), and no review count. The nearest thing to a proxy is the owner's line "since the
  beginning of my nursing" — which is a career *reference with no length attached*, so it is not
  even the practitioner-career-length rung that would keep the row at B. Under the 5 Nov 2026
  evidence ladder, no proxy of any kind parks a row at C, and that is what this is.
- **MUST-HAVE 2 — THE NATUROPATHY LABEL, CHECKED AND DISMISSED.** Search returned this clinic's
  homepage under the title "Skin & Naturopathy Clinic in Gold Coast", which is a must-have 2 and
  must-have 1 alarm (the ICP fails a clinic running a naturopathy arm receipted to third-party
  plans). I read the homepage for it: **"naturopathy" appears only in the page title and meta
  tags, and not one naturopathic service appears in the body text or the treatment menu.** That is
  the "a label is not a finding" shape exactly, and I am recording the dismissal rather than the
  label. Must-have 2 passes. *Note the mirror rule, 9 Nov 2026: dismissing the parked reason is not
  by itself a pass — so I also read the menu, and the menu is injectables and skin, start to finish.*
- **A CAVEAT THAT MATTERS MORE THAN THE GRADE: THE SITE IS SPAM-INJECTED.** The homepage carries
  hidden keyword strings and links wholly unrelated to a skin clinic — "1Win", "Tower Rush",
  "chicken road casino", "Flappy Bird" — and several internal links point at targets that do not
  match their labels ("Rejuran" resolves to a fat-dissolving URL). Under the sourcing brief's rule
  for a compromised page, nothing attested **only** by that page is recordable as the clinic's own
  words, and it is not ours to fix or to mention to them. So: the address and the mailbox are safe
  because the **contact page** attests to both independently and the two pages agree. The owner's
  name (Diana Cern, AHPRA Registered Nurse and Cosmetic Injector) and the booking platform
  (**Timely**, `bookings.gettimely.com/dianacernaesthetics/bb/book`) rest on the compromised page
  alone and are recorded here with that caveat rather than promoted into a row.
- **Other findings worth keeping:** free consultation offered ("Fair Price and Free Consultation")
  — a real dormant pool. A "We accept" block exists but its contents are an unreadable image, so
  payment methods are unknown. Timely is a named practice system and would be a grade-A signal if
  it were attested anywhere else.
- **The one check that releases this row:** a review count, a founding year or a copyright range on
  a page of its own site that is **not** the compromised homepage. I did not guess a path for an
  About or reviews page — the brief's measurement is that three of four guessed paths return client
  errors, and evidence found on a compromised page would be unrecordable anyway.
- **Not a browser-visit candidate.** Nothing is obfuscated and the mailbox is already in hand; the
  blocker is qualification evidence, not tooling.

  general-dentistry page lists fourteen service groups, and they are general and restorative

  removals; root canal treatment; crowns, bridges and veneers; dentures including
  mini-implant-supported; extractions and wisdom teeth removal; implants; mouthguards, nightguards,
  TMJ splints and anti-snoring devices; children's dentistry; **procedures under general
  anaesthesia**; laser dentistry. Injectables are one line in that list ("dento-facial aesthetics,
  including lip augmentation and muscle relaxants"), and the only named practitioner, **Dr Wilhelm
  Koch**, is a dentist (Australian Academy of Dento-Facial Aesthetics, International Team of
  Implantology). This is a general dental practice with a cosmetic arm, not an injectables-led
  clinic or med spa — a disease-and-restorative caseload under general anaesthesia is substance,
  not a word on a page.
- **This one was decided by result titles before any fetch, exactly as the brief predicted.** The
  batched domain search returned the title **"General Dentistry"** on this domain, and that single
  title is what told me to read the dental menu rather than the aesthetics copy. It cost zero
  fetches and it turned out to be the whole answer.
- **AU/NZ must-have 6:** (a) the address was read off the business's own contact page, not a
  directory; (b) **no** "no unsolicited commercial email" notice and no anti-spam wording on either
  page read, and no privacy policy is linked to check. Both findings recorded; both are moot
  against a must-have 2 failure proven in the clinic's own words.
- **Must-have 4 would have passed**, for the record: the footer reads "Copyright 2014 North Hobart
  Dental", and a bare copyright year at least three years old is a usable dated artifact under the
  8 Nov 2026 rung — twelve years, which is also enough trading time on substance. The row fails on
  what it sells and how it bills, not on its age.
- **Do not revisit. Not a browser-visit candidate** — nothing is hidden; the mailbox is in hand and
  the business is disqualified.

---

## What this recovery taught us

**The six were correctly described as a block and wrongly described as untouched.** Every one of
the six was dropped on the single-operator rule and nothing else — the premise held — but the
September file had already half-opened one of them, and the recorded doubt it left turned out to be
the right doubt. See the corrections below.

**One in six was sendable, and the budget shape was the opposite of what was feared.** Searches
were cheap and fetches were the binding cost: **3 searches, 11 fetches**, where the brief budgeted
8 searches to 12 fetches. The batched `allowed_domains` guess resolved **four of six domains in a
single call** and, more valuably, handed over three findings from result titles alone at zero fetch
cost: DC Aesthetics is on the Gold Coast, Newcastle Cosmetic Doctor is Dr Bart Scanlon's and is in
New South Wales, and **Hobart Facial Aesthetics has a "General Dentistry" page** — which is the
fact that disqualified it. The title-reading technique decided a clinic outright for the second run
in a row.

**And the invisible-miss caveat fired, exactly as warned.** Two of my six guesses returned nothing:
`drsarahsparks.com.au` was right and simply did not surface on that generic query, and
`sapphireappearancemedicine.co.nz` was **wrong** — the real domain is **`sapphire.net.nz`**, which
no amount of name-guessing would have produced. A short, non-descriptive domain on a clinic with a
long descriptive name is the failure case for domain guessing, and the only cure was a name search.
Both were recovered for one search each.

**The AU/NZ consent screen cost almost nothing and refused nothing.** Six clinics, eleven pages
read, **zero** "no unsolicited commercial email" notices, zero anti-spam statements and zero
refusals of any kind. Not one site in this group even published a privacy policy to check — five of
the six have none at all, which is a different finding from "the policy was clean" and is recorded
that way on every entry. The two marketing phrases I did find — "Join our mailing list" and
"Updates about our products" — are invitations to receive, and are quoted verbatim above precisely
so nobody later reads them as the refusal they are not. The running tally in the ICP, now past
eighty clinics, stands: **no AU, NZ or Canadian clinic has yet been found refusing unsolicited
commercial email.** Budget must-have 6 as nearly free and expect it to pass.

**Must-have 4 was the binding constraint again, and in an unexpected market.** Two of the six — DC
Aesthetics and Dr Sarah Sparks — publish **no dated or quantified artifact whatsoever**, not even a
copyright year. That is the fifth-or-later measurement of the ICP's affluent-referral-market
pattern, and it arrived here from Australian coastal cities rather than from Britain or an American
suburb. It is also a fourth distinct variety of the same blind spot: Britain's clinics are busy and
do not print the number, New Jersey's print a broken one, and **these two print no footer at all** —
small WordPress and SiteOrigin sites with no copyright line, which the ladder reads as "no trading
history" when what it has actually read is a theme default.

**The real surprise was neither search nor fetch budget: it was site health.** Two of six sites are
materially broken or compromised. DC Aesthetics' homepage is **spam-injected** with casino keyword
strings and mislabelled internal links, which under the brief's compromised-page rule makes its
owner name and its Timely instance unrecordable from that page — the best grade-A signal in the
run, unusable. Dr Sarah Sparks' site has every internal link pointing at `#`. Neither is a fetch
failure, neither is on the browser-visit list, and neither is something the ladder or the must-haves
have a rung for. **Expect to spend a fetch on a second page not to find more, but to corroborate
what the first page said.**

**Nothing from this run goes on the browser-visit list, and that is itself worth recording.** Not
one of the six was Cloudflare-obfuscated, CleanTalk-masked or interstitial-blocked. Three publish a
real plain-text mailbox and three publish none at all. **Where email fails in this group it fails
because the clinic published nothing, which no browser fixes** — so the group generated two
form-or-phone rows for a non-email channel and zero browser jobs.

---

## Corrections to the commission and to our own file

**1. "They were never opened at all" is wrong for one of the six.** **Coastal Skin & Laser
(Tewantin)** had already been partially opened. near-misses.md lines 2604-2616 carry an entry for
**Nurse Laura** at `nurselaura.com.au`, working at the same address, which records the host clinic's
street address ("4/84 Poinciana Avenue, Tewantin"), names Dr Andrew Spall, and flags that Laura's
"skin cancer nursing interests, dermoscopy and benign lesion removal" put the cash-pay must-have in
doubt. So one of the six had an address and a recorded must-have doubt in our files before this run
— and **that doubt was correct**, which is the part worth keeping. It is also a partial exception to
"none of the six has a domain recorded anywhere": `nurselaura.com.au` is an associated domain
reaching the same practice, though not the clinic's own.

**2. A seventh name sits in the same bullets and is not recoverable.** **Dr Terrence Scamp** is
listed beside DC Aesthetics under the identical "single operators" heading. He is a Gold Coast
plastic surgeon and is **disqualified** under ICP v2 (must-have 1 and the plastic-surgery
disqualification), not recoverable. Our file already flags this and warns that the bullet "must not
be re-read as one rule". Flagged again because the bullet still reads as one list.

**3. Our file's own count differs from itself.** The 24 Sep NZ/regional-AU section says of its
block "**these five** have never been opened", while the recovery-candidate section at line 13705
says "**six** AU/NZ single operators, never opened". Both are right about different sets — DC
Aesthetics is in the Australian section, the other five in the NZ/regional-AU one — but a reader
grepping either number alone gets a different answer. Not an error, just a seam.

**4. Nothing else in the premise was overstated.** Every one of the six was recorded as dropped on
the single-operator rule, no entry claimed a published address without printing one, and no entry
claimed an email that did not exist. The specific September failure mode the brief warned about —
a heading asserting "real published emails" with no address, domain or URL written down anywhere —
**does not appear in these six entries.** The brief's suspicion was reasonable and, this time, the
file was honest.

## What this market taught me

**1. THE BRIEF IS WRONG THAT "NOTHING IN THIS MARKET HAS BEEN SWEPT", and this is the most
important correction in the run.** `near-misses.md` line 394 carries a whole section headed
**"Mid-Atlantic — DC, Northern Virginia, Maryland, Richmond (16 Oct 2026)"**, which put **eighteen
rows** into the pipeline and left sixteen named near-misses, four of them inside Montgomery County
(Butterfly Medical Spa in Rockville, Aesthetic Artistry and NoBe in North Bethesda, Life Med
Institute) and three more in the northern Virginia ring (The District Injector and Pure Med Spa in
McLean, Purity Spa Med in Arlington). What was genuinely unswept is **Montgomery County proper
below the Rockville/North Bethesda line** — Bethesda, Chevy Chase, Potomac, Olney, Gaithersburg,
Silver Spring, Burtonsville all returned zero prior hits — and **Arlington and Vienna were already
held as pipeline rows 205 and 212.** So the market was half-worked, not untouched, and the grep
that would have shown it is `grep -n "Mid-Atlantic" near-misses.md`. **A "nothing has been swept"
claim in a brief should be re-greped, not believed** — mine cost nothing because the grep came
first, but a worker who trusted it would have re-fetched Butterfly and NoBe.

**2. YES — A MARYLAND CLINIC WAS ALREADY IN THE FILE, EXACTLY AS WARNED, AND THE WARNING IS
ACCURATE.** `bellablissmedspa.com` is pipeline row 211, "Bella Bliss Med Spa, Rockville, MD", grade
B, added 16 Oct — so it was NOT put there by the Long Island misfire; the misfire merely rediscovered
it. The misfire's own note names five further Rockville MD businesses it dragged in, and **I worked
one of them: The Beauty Bay, which is now an accepted B row.** The other four are **ReNew You**,
**Aesthetic & Dermatology Center**, **Faulkner Plastic Surgery** (plastic surgery, must-have 1) and
**The Medical Skin Clinic** — the first and the last are unworked and are the cheapest outstanding
leads in this market. I ran the same-name check in the direction the brief asked: every Rockville
candidate was confirmed by its **postal ZIP (20850, 20852)** and **240/301 area codes**, which are
Montgomery County, not Nassau County.

**3. THE LABEL TEST FIRED ONCE AND THE CLINIC FAILED — the first time in the affluent-suburb
series, and it does NOT overturn the Westchester finding.** The brief carried in the expectation
that "dermatology" in a wealthy suburb is a hiring credential, cleared five of five in Westchester.
Here it fired once, on **Capital Laser & Skin Care of Chevy Chase**, and the substance was there:
three board-certified physicians, **"Skin Cancer" listed as a treated concern**, a vascular laser
and hyperhidrosis. So the Westchester rule worked **exactly as designed** — it told me to read the
menu instead of the noun, and the menu failed the clinic. **A test that reverses the default five
times and confirms it the sixth is a working test, not a broken one.** Separately and in the same
shape, **The Beauty Bay's medical director's title contains "Surgeon"** with no surgical procedure
anywhere on the menu — hiring credential, cleared, row accepted. **Two label cases, opposite
outcomes, both decided off the treatment menu.**

**4. MUST-HAVE 4 ON EVIDENCE IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT HERE TOO — A FIFTH MEASUREMENT, AND THE
RATIO IS THE WORST YET. ONLY 3 OF THE 15 BUSINESSES WHOSE OWN PAGES I READ PUBLISHED A DATED OR
QUANTIFIED ARTIFACT ABOUT THE BUSINESS — 1 IN 5.** Those three: MedRevive ("Founded in 2010"), Tiam Spa ("Based on 166 reviews")
and The Beauty Bay ("90 verified reviews"). **Four of my five C rows are C on must-have 4 evidence
alone** — Moksha, Aluna, Artmedica, and Defy Aesthetic (which is not in the near-misses because it
has a published mailbox and sits in the JSON at C). Britain, Fairfield County, Long Island, northern
New Jersey, and now the Washington DC affluent ring: **five markets, one shape.** This is a market
type, not a nationality, and it was right to carry it in as an expectation rather than report it as
a surprise. **I did not pad a single row to compensate.** **Market type: affluent, referral-driven,
federal-professional suburb — the stingiest publishers measured so far, and nine sendable-or-parked
rows out of 22 businesses is a good market behind a thin grade mix.**

**5. THE "0 COUNTER BESIDE REAL TESTIMONIALS" CASE HAS A NEW COUSIN HERE, AND IT IS WORSE: THE
COUNTER THAT CONTRADICTS ITSELF.** New Jersey's broken widgets printed "0" beside real reviews.
**MedRevive prints three mutually inconsistent numbers** — "Founded in 2010", a "20 Year Of
Experience" counter, "over 25 years of combined experience" — plus a "10 Happy Returning Clients"
counter that is obviously a placeholder. The 9 Nov operational rule ("do not let a broken number
beat a readable page") extends cleanly: **prefer the specific, checkable claim over the counter
widget.** "Founded in 2010" is a date somebody typed on purpose; "20 Year Of Experience" is a theme
demo nobody edited. That is the strongest must-have 4 evidence in this sweep and it was sitting
beside two numbers that would have made a careless reader distrust it.

**6. THE PRIVACY-POLICY ADDRESS ROUTE: I SPENT IT ZERO TIMES AND THE COUNT IS ZERO FROM ZERO — AND
THAT IS A REAL DATA POINT, NOT AN OMISSION.** The brief asked me to spend it and record the count,
and the honest answer is that **the rule never came up**, because the market did not produce its
precondition. **Of the 15 businesses whose own page I read, 10 published a mailbox on that first
page in plain characters** — Fresh Face, The Beauty Bay, MedRevive, Estar, Aluna, Moksha, Tiam,
Angels, Artmedica, Defy. One more (beBold) published a masked one. The policy rule triggers on a
*silent* homepage, and I met only **four** silent homepages (Juve, Glow AMC, Luxe, Capital Laser),
**three of which failed a second must-have independently**, so spending a policy fetch on them would
have bought a C row at best on a shared budget. The one where it would have been the right call is
**Juve**, and I have named the URL above so the next person spends one fetch rather than a search
plus a fetch. **The finding, which is about the geography line rather than the mechanism: this
market is overwhelmingly EMAIL-FIRST** — 10 of 15 publishing in plain text on the first page read,
the best rate in any market in the file that I can see — **which is exactly why the policy route had
nothing to do.** The mechanism the file has
confirmed five times says the rule's yield tracks how email-first a market is; an email-first market
therefore produces a yield of *nothing needed*, not a yield of zero. **"Mountain West and South yes,
coasts no" is dead, and this market shows why replacing it with any geography is a mistake: the
predictor is publication habit, and here the habit made the rule redundant.**

**7. THE MAIN-STREET QUERY SHAPE WORKS, AND THE BRIEF NAMED THE RIGHT STREETS.** One query on
"Wisconsin Avenue Bethesda Row Old Georgetown Road Potomac Village" returned **Fresh Face Med Spa at
8311 Wisconsin Avenue** — now an accepted B row with Jane, memberships and a loyalty programme —
which the plain "Bethesda med spa" query had not surfaced. Three of my nine accepted rows sit on a
named retail spine: **8311 Wisconsin Avenue** (Bethesda), **321 B Main Street, Kentlands**
(Gaithersburg), **Cabin John Village** (Potomac). The equivalent for this county is **retail
village + Main Street**, not downtown.

**8. THE OUTER COUNTY IS EMPTY, AND I WOULD NOT SPEND ANOTHER QUERY ON IT.** A stacked query on
**Germantown, Clarksburg, Kensington and Chevy Chase** returned **not one qualifying clinic domain
in ten results** — four dermatology or cosmetic-surgery practices, a day spa, a skincare studio, a
US News doctor directory and a **Medicaid provider directory PDF**. Wheaton returned nothing on any
query. These are not under-searched; they are towns whose aesthetic demand is served from Bethesda,
Rockville and Silver Spring. **Germantown, Clarksburg, Kensington, Wheaton and Chevy Chase proper:
worked out, nothing to find.** Chevy Chase has exactly two aesthetic businesses with their own
domains and both are above (Juve, no email; Capital Laser, disqualified).

**9. THE FEHB / CAREFIRST / MEDICARE WARNING DID NOT FIRE ONCE IN THE WAY IT WAS EXPECTED TO — IT
FIRED SIDEWAYS.** I read every menu specifically for scheme acronyms, per the NYSHIP case, in the
most federal-employment-heavy metro in the country. **Not one clinic printed FEHB, CareFirst,
Medicare or any federal-employee plan beside a service line — zero of 22.** What DID fail on
must-have 2 was **Glow Aesthetics & Medical Center**, and it failed on a **Primary Care menu heading
plus "If not covered by insurance" against lab pricing** — the same structural failure (a
non-discretionary, third-party-reimbursed arm bolted to an aesthetics menu) arriving through a
*service line* rather than a *scheme name*. **The expectation was right about the region and wrong
about the tell.** In a government-professional market the reimbursed arm is a primary-care or
hormone clinic, not a named insurance plan on a treatment list. Two clinics flagged **HSA/FSA
acceptance** (Juve, Luxe) and that is the patient's own pre-tax money — **not** a must-have 2
failure, and it is going to keep reading like one, so it is worth the sentence.

**10. WHAT I RAN OUT OF: candidates, not budget.** 7 searches and 18 fetches against a shared pool
of about 16 and 50. I stopped because the last two searches returned dermatology practices,
directories and a Medicaid PDF rather than new independents — the county's independent aesthetic
sector is roughly fifteen businesses deep and I opened most of it. **The cheapest remaining work in
this market, in order:** (a) **ReNew You** and **The Medical Skin Clinic**, both Rockville MD, named
by the Long Island misfire and never opened — one search each; (b) one fetch on
**`https://juve.beauty/privacy-policy/`** for an address plus a founding year; (c) one fetch on
**`https://www.alunaaesthetics.com/locations/bethesda-md`**, an SEO suburb page that per the 9 Nov
rule carries the whole footer and bio, to try to release Aluna from C.

## FIRST, A CORRECTION TO MY OWN BRIEF, because it changes how this run should be read

My commissioning brief said *"A Chicago pass on 8 Nov 2026 covered Lake Forest and some of the
metro"* and that *"the towns above are where the unworked ground is."* **That is not what the file
says.** The 8 Nov Chicago section states its market as assigned in its own first lines:

> Winnetka, Wilmette, Glencoe, Kenilworth, Highland Park, Lake Forest, Northbrook, Glenview,
> Evanston · Hinsdale, Oak Brook, Clarendon Hills, Western Springs, La Grange, Naperville,
> Wheaton, Geneva.

**That is thirteen of my sixteen assigned towns, not "Lake Forest and some of the metro."** It
spent 16 searches and 46 fetches on them and produced pipeline rows 1046-1061. Only **three** towns
on my list were genuinely outside it: **Deerfield, Northfield and Burr Ridge** — and Northfield had
in fact been reached incidentally (Trio Med Spa is a Northfield near-miss in that file).

So the real unworked ground was: **Burr Ridge** (where 3 of my 6 rows came from), **Deerfield**,
and the four towns the 8 Nov worker itself flagged as unfinished — **Northbrook and Glencoe**
("produced no independent of their own … worth one query each") and **Clarendon Hills and Western
Springs** ("produced nothing at all"). I worked those, plus Evanston, which was in the 8 Nov market
but yielded zero sendable rows. That is why this run's yield is six and not sixty: it is a
second pass over largely-swept ground, by design once the file is read, and it should be judged
against that rather than against a fresh metro.

## What this market taught me, and which conventions it moved

**1. Must-have 4 on EVIDENCE is the binding constraint, confirmed for a FIFTH time and in the same
shape.** **Four of my six rows are C, and all four are C on must-have 4 alone** — nothing else
failed them. Of the nine in-market businesses I read in full, **only two published a dated or
quantified artifact about the business**: Melamed's "113 Reviews" and MedAndSpa's "jointly open
MedAndSpa in 2017" — and *both of those are near-misses with no email.* **The two strongest trading
histories in the market belong to the two clinics we cannot reach.** Britain, Fairfield County,
Long Island, northern New Jersey and now the Chicago suburbs: five markets, one shape. I carried the
expectation in rather than discovering it, and that was the right thing to carry — it meant I parked
the four without padding any of them and without spending a second fetch hunting for a review count
that is not there.

**2. The copyright-year rung did almost all the parking, and that is worth noticing.** Of my four C
rows, three were parked by a **bare current-or-recent-year copyright**: © 2026 (Aesthoria, Arabella),
© 2025 (LAB), and Renova has **no copyright year at all**. Not one of the four publishes a review
count. So in this market the ladder is not sorting clinics by trading history at all — it is sorting
them by **whether anyone bothered to print a number on the page**, which is the open question the
ICP already flags. I am not proposing a change; I am adding the fifth measurement to it.

**3. A new-ish wrinkle on must-have 4, offered because I had to decide it twice in one run and
reached opposite answers.** Aesthoria and The Injection Vault are near-identical on the ladder — both
publish only a practitioner's career length, both on Moxie, both single-site, both with a founder
named. I graded Aesthoria **B** and The Injection Vault **C**, and the only thing separating them is
that **The Injection Vault ships unreplaced builder placeholder text in two of its three
testimonials** ("Maybe you want to launch a business"). **Proposed rung, in the spirit of the "broken
widget" rung from New Jersey but pointing the other way: unreplaced template placeholder copy in the
social-proof slot is positive evidence of a RECENT LAUNCH, and it should beat the career-length
rung.** New Jersey's lesson was *do not let a broken number beat a readable page*; this is the
converse — *do not let a career length stand in for a trading history when the page itself is still
wearing its factory settings.* If that is wrong, the fix is to promote Injection Vault to B, and the
row says so.

**4. Platform concentration in Burr Ridge is MOXIE, which is a different answer from eleven miles
away, and that is the per-market rule holding.** The 8 Nov sweep of the same metro counted
**Aesthetic Record ×6** as the clear leader across the North Shore and western suburbs, with Moxie
appearing exactly once (Face Forward was Mangomint). In the four Burr Ridge-area independents I
opened, **Moxie appears three times** — Aesthoria, The Injection Vault and Renova (Northbrook) — with
Zenoti once (LAB) and Mangomint once (MedAndSpa), and **no Aesthetic Record at all.** Two readings,
and I think the second is right: either the two samples are too small, or **Moxie is the platform the
newest cohort of single-nurse clinics is launching on**, which fits — it is a turnkey
med-spa-in-a-box, and all three Moxie clinics are also the three with no trading-history evidence.
**If that is right, seeing Moxie is a weak NEGATIVE signal on must-have 4 even though it is a
positive signal on "a queryable patient list exists".** Worth watching rather than acting on.
Platform concentration being a per-market fact is confirmed again; I would add that it may be a
per-*cohort* fact inside a market.

**5. THE MAIN-STREET QUERY SHAPE FAILED, AND MY BRIEF ASSERTED IT WOULD WORK.** I was told
*"the main-street query shape works in affluent suburbs: here that means Green Bay Road, Central
Street Evanston, Sheridan Road, Hubbard Woods, First Street Highland Park, Hinsdale Village, Oak
Brook Center."* I spent two queries on it. `Green Bay Road Sheridan Road Wilmette Kenilworth Glencoe
skin clinic injectables nurse founder` returned **zero in-market clinics** — it returned a
Pleasantville NY clinic, an Oklahoma City clinic, a Wisconsin hospital group, a Grand Junction CO
clinic and a Greenwich CT dermatology practice. `Central Street Evanston Dempster Davis Street`
returned two job boards, a CVS MinuteClinic and three `areas-served` SEO pages. **And this is not
new information: the 8 Nov Chicago sweep already recorded that the district-association and
main-street technique "did not work" on the North Shore and that "no business-improvement-district or
main-street association index surfaced at all."** So the brief asserted as a live technique something
the file had already measured as failing in this exact market. **The North Shore's shopping streets
have strong social identities and no indexed trade presence** — Tulsa's Brookside result does not
transfer here, and the 8 Nov note that the neighbourhood technique "works on names locals trade
under, not on names estate agents use" is the right diagnosis: North Shore clinics address
themselves by *town*, not by street.

**What DID work, for the third sweep running:** **four unquoted town names plus two modifiers, with
"owner" or "founder" as one of them.** Five of my seven discovery queries in that shape returned real
clinic domains, and `Glencoe Western Springs Clarendon Hills Burr Ridge aesthetics injectables clinic
owner founder` alone produced three of my six rows.

**6. The privacy-policy address rule went ONE FROM THREE here, and the one it found was the only
mailbox that clinic publishes anywhere.** Renova Medspa publishes `info@renovamedspail.com` on its
privacy policy and nowhere else — without that fetch, Northbrook has no independent in our files at
all. The two misses were MedAndSpa (policy nominates **no** route, phone only, body last modified
2022) and Melamed (**mode seven** — nominates an email route and omits the address). **Combined with
8 Nov's two-from-four, Illinois now stands at 3 of 7, which is almost exactly the one-in-three the
brief budgets for the Mountain West.** The mechanism held in all three misses, for the sixth
consecutive confirmation: a phone number or a postal address satisfied the data-request duty. **And
the geography line failed again, in the clinic's favour this time** — a Midwest industrial-suburb
market publishing at Arizona rates. I agree with the brief that geography should be dropped as a
predictor and the rule spent unconditionally; here it bought a row for one fetch.

**7. The privacy-policy PROCESSOR-LIST technique paid nothing in three attempts, which is worth
recording against the 8 Nov claim.** The 8 Nov sweep promoted it on one spectacular instance (DK
Aesthetics naming seven processors including Resend and Google Sheets). I read three Illinois
policies on this pass and **none of them named a single processor the marketing pages had not already
given me.** MedAndSpa's listed only the vendors already visible in its own footer; Renova's names
none at all, referring only to unnamed "third-party payment processors"; Melamed's names none. **It
is a free look because you are reading the page anyway, so keep doing it — but it is a lottery, not a
technique, and one DK Aesthetics does not make it a rule.**

**8. The dermatology label test did NOT fire once in this market, which is itself a measurement.**
The 9 Nov Westchester finding was that the word is a hiring credential in a wealthy suburb and the
test cleared five of five clinics. In nine businesses read here, **not one used the word
"dermatology" about itself.** What this market does instead is the *plastic-surgery* version:
**MedAndSpa's medical director is a double board-certified plastic surgeon**, and I cleared it on
substance (no surgical line on the menu, nothing insurance-billed) exactly as the label rule
requires. The 8 Nov sweep ruled out nine dermatology and plastic-surgery practices by name in the
same metro, so the specialty density is real — it just sits in *separate businesses* here rather than
inside med spas' copy. **The operational version for this metro: screen the specialty of the
business before its scale, and screen the medical director's specialty against the MENU rather than
against his credentials.**

**9. Two look-alikes and one near-trap worth adding to the running lists.**
The look-alike that almost cost a row is the **gmail-on-own-site** case: Arabella publishes
`arabellaboutiquemedspa@gmail.com` as a `mailto:` on its own contact page. That is the third and
fourth Illinois instance after Radiant A and Oakbrook Advanced on 8 Nov, and **the 8 Nov worker's
suggestion that this case be named explicitly in the ICP's seven-item list still has not been
actioned.** It passes both of the ruling's tests — published on their own site, received by them —
and it should stop being re-argued each sweep. The near-trap is **Beauty with Bubbly's Open Graph
description saying "Northfield, IL" over a postal address that says Glenview** — the second instance
of the meta-versus-postal mismatch in this metro after Mandala Aesthetics, inside one state both
times. And the new same-name town is **Northfield**, which has a Minnesota twin that outranks the
Illinois one.

**10. One thing the brief got exactly right and I want on the record:** *"an individual suburb or
`areas-served` SEO page carries the full site footer — block the page sets from crowding a query, read
any single one you land on."* Both halves fired. Reclaim MedSpa's and Dermaluxe's page sets took five
query slots between them, and the one `areas-served` page I tried to read was the only route to an
otherwise invisible clinic. It failed on `robots_disallowed` rather than on the technique, which is
why Dermaluxe is on the browser list rather than in the bin.

Only one, and it is cheap:

- **Dermaluxe Aesthetics** — `https://www.dermaluxeaesthetics.com/about-us/areas-served/evanston/`
  (or the Glencoe equivalent). **`robots_disallowed`**, so a fetch is refused and a person's browser
  sees it normally. One page-load would give the mailbox, the treatment menu, the owner, the base
  town and the site count at once, because an `areas-served` page carries the whole site footer.
  **It is the only untried route into Evanston**, which three queries have otherwise failed to open.
  Nothing is known about this business yet — it is unscreened, not near-missed.

**Nothing else from this run needs a browser.** The two best clinics in the market (MedAndSpa,
Melamed) are **silence** and **mode seven** respectively, and no browser recovers either; they are
phone or direct-message prospects. The three Chicago-area browser candidates already on the list from
8 Nov — Dermatique (Cloudflare), La BeauTe (client-side), Blue Seas (client-side) — were deliberately
not re-fetched, as instructed, and remain the highest-value items in this metro.

## 5. Not reachable by fetch — a tool failure, not a clinic finding

### `juvenate.com/providers/` — "All 380 Med Spas — Philadelphia to the Lehigh Valley"
- **Fetch failed with `client_error` and nothing was retrieved.** This read in the search snippet
  like the single highest-yield directory index available in this market — 380 named providers
  across exactly our geography — and it is unreadable. One fetch lost. **Do not buy it again.**

### `mainlinetoday.com/best-of-the-main-line/best-main-line-winners/`
- Fetched **deliberately** as a names source, on the reasoning that a reader-voted best-of is
  closer to a human "best in town" list than to a paid listicle, and that blocking a domain in a
  query does not forbid reading one page of it on purpose — the same distinction the 9 Nov rule
  draws for `areas-served` page sets.
- **It returned the intro, the critics' names, a party advert and a newsletter form, and NOT ONE
  WINNER.** The category lists render client-side. The page confirms it is a reader poll
  ("our readers' ballots and elimination round voting"), so the reasoning was sound and the
  **mechanism** defeated it. One fetch lost. **Do not buy it again.**
- **This extends the 8 Nov city-magazine hazard rather than repeating it.** That note says a
  sponsored city-magazine listicle is a coin flip on quality *that you cannot assess before
  paying*. This one is worse and in a new way: **a genuine reader poll can be unreadable
  entirely**, so the hazard is not only editorial but technical.

---

## What this market taught me

**The Main Line is a real market with a thin top end, and the constraint is exactly the one the
brief said to expect — but it is not the only one.**

**Twenty-three businesses were researched. Ten became rows (2 A, 4 B, 4 C). Thirteen did not.**
Of the thirteen: **seven fail must-have 5** (four Cloudflare or robots, three total silence),
**four are outright disqualifications**, and **two were already ours.** Of the four parked C rows,
**three are C on must-have 4 and nothing else** — so the brief's prediction held, and must-have 4
on evidence remains the binding constraint in an affluent referral-driven suburb. **Report the
market type with the mix: this is a stingy market full of good clinics, not a weak one.**

**But must-have 5 was heavier here than in the other three suburbs, and the reason is specific.**
Four of the seven unreachable clinics are **Cloudflare or robots cases** — recoverable in a
browser — and three of those four (Essent, Bala Better Health, La-Mon'e) are among the best
businesses in the market. **The Main Line's strong clinics protect their mailboxes.** That is a
different failure from Long Island's broken widgets or Britain's unprinted review counts, and it
means **the browser-visit list is where this market's value actually sits.** Essent Spa alone —
physician-owner named, 167 reviews, a 2018 copyright and 2016 testimonials — is worth more than
two of my accepted rows.

**Four things I would hand to the next worker:**

1. **A dead clinic is holding four towns hostage.** `a360medspa.com` has permanently closed and its
   SEO page set still ranks for Berwyn, Devon, Villanova and Bryn Mawr. Block it. Berwyn, Devon,
   Gladwyne, Narberth, Rosemont and Paoli produced **no own-domain clinic of their own** in this
   sweep, and this is at least part of why.
2. **The privacy policy is a must-have 2 screen, not only an address fetch.** `dermguy.com`'s
   homepage carried no insurance language whatsoever and its policy collects insurance carrier
   and ID numbers and shares PHI with insurers. **That is must-have 2 decided off a page we already
   spend a fetch on**, and it is the cheapest way yet found to catch a cash-pay-looking clinic that
   bills. Read the policy's data-collection list for insurance words on the same pass as the
   mailbox and the processor list.
3. **An ownership change resets must-have 4, and the footer will not tell you.** Lily & Oak
   advertises "8+ Years on the Main Line" and a "Since 2018" badge; its About page says the premises
   opened in 2018 **as a different business**, that the current owner bought it in 2025, and that
   she relaunched it in **February 2026**. Nine months of her own list. This is a **fifth** variety
   the evidence ladder cannot tell apart — history that belongs to a **previous owner** — and it
   sits beside the honest C, the unprinted history, the broken widget and the missing footer. It
   cost one extra fetch and saved a wrong B.
4. **Suburban Square and Eagle Village are same-name traps, not just main streets.** The
   main-street query shape works here (Germantown Avenue and State Street each produced an accepted
   row, Lancaster Avenue produced two), but a shopping-centre name built from common words pulled a
   Georgia clinic with a perfectly readable address into a Main Line query. Read the state in the
   postal address.
